title: Introduction to FAARFIELD
html:
FAARFIELD is a computer program for airport pavement thickness design. It implements both layered elastic-based and three-dimensional finite element-based design procedures developed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for new and overlay design of flexible and rigid pavements. The thickness design procedures implemented in the program are based on the FAA airport pavement thickness design standards in the Advisory Circular (AC) 150/5320-6. FAARFIELD is the product of a long process of development that began with efforts in the 1970's to produce a rational design method based on mechanistic-empirical principles and employing computer technology, including layered elastic design (LED). Some historical references that provide background on the development of the FAARFIELD design procedures include:

Barker, W.R., and Brabston, W.N., (1975). Development of a Structural Design Procedure for Flexible Pavements. Report No. FAA-RD-74-199.

Parker, F., Jr., Barker, W.R., Gunkel, R.C., and Odom, E.C. (1977). Development of a Structural Design Procedure for Rigid Airport Pavements. Report No. FAA- RD- 77- 81.

Rollings, R.S., (1988). Design of Overlays for Rigid Airport Pavements. Report No. DOT/FAA/PM-87/19.

Barker, W.R., and Gonzalez, C.R. (1991). Pavement Design by Elastic Layer Theory, Proceedings. ASCE Conference on Airplane/Pavement Interaction, Kansas City.

Copies of the FAA reports may be obtained from the National Technical Information Service, Alexandria, VA (www.NTIS.gov).

FAARFIELD represents a significant departure from previous FAA standards that were in place from the 1960's through 2009. Apart from the procedures being implemented as a computer program instead of as nomographs, the main change in pavement design from the user's perspective is that the "design airplane" concept has been replaced by design for fatigue failure expressed in terms of a "cumulative damage factor" (CDF) using Miner's rule. Also, the major material property of the pavement layers is now uniformly expressed as an elastic modulus instead of the previous CBR (California Bearing Ratio) for flexible pavements or k value for rigid pavements. Formulas for transforming CBR and k values to modulus values are provided where appropriate in the documentation. The program automatically converts CBR and k to modulus.

FAARFIELD belongs to the category of mechanistic-empirical (M-E) design procedures, meaning that it combines an engineering-mechanical structural analysis (layered elastic or finite element) with empirical failure models. While FAARFIELD is more rational than previous procedures, a considerable amount of engineering judgment is still required to produce valid designs. Designs produced by FAARFIELD should comply with the detailed requirements and recommendations of AC 150/5320-6, however, the program does not automatically satisfy all these requirements. The recommendations in the AC should be followed in the selection of input parameters. It is the designer's responsibility to use the program and the advisory circular in conjunction with each other.

FAARFIELD 2.0 is the latest standard thickness design software accompanying AC 150/5320-6G Airport Pavement Design and Evaluation. It is written in Visual Basic 2019™ with .NET Framework 4.8. The program operates in the Microsoft Windows™ environment. The program includes a structural response module consisting of two subprograms: LEAF and FAASR3D. Both LEAF and FAASR3D are loaded by FAARFIELD when the program is run; they are not visible to the user.

LEAF is a layered elastic computational program written in Visual Basic 2019™ and implemented as a Microsoft Windows™ dynamic link library (DLL). FAASR3D is a three-dimensional finite element (3D-FE) analysis program written in Visual Basic 2019™. FAASR3D replaces the FAA-modified version of the 3D-FE software program NIKE3D, which was used in all previous FAARFIELD versions under the terms of a software sharing agreement with the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) of the US Department of Energy, the original developer of NIKE3D. FAAMesh is the part of FAASR3D that generates finite element mesh models for analysis by FAASR3D, and is implemented as a separate DLL.

FAARFIELD 2.0 is completely rebuilt with a new graphical user interface (GUI) and programmed with a new 3D-FE analysis library, FAASR3D, replacing the NIKE3D Fortran program used in previous versions. FAARFIELD 2.0 is also integrated with the Aircraft Classification Rating-Pavement Classification Rating (ACR-PCR) method in accordance with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) procedure. The internal vehicle library was updated to reflect the current aircraft fleet. Individual aircraft information has been updated based on information from airplane manufactures. The User Defined Aircraft (UDA) system was restructured to enhance the flexibility.

title: Installation of FAARFIELD 2.0
html:
Administrative rights are required to install FAARFIELD 2.0. Once installed, the user does not require Administrative rights to run FAARFIELD 2.0.

Installation of FAARFIELD 2.0 is launched by double clicking on the file FAARFIELD.Installer.msi. The installation process consists of a series of dialog boxes similar to the one shown in Figure 3-1. Follow to prompts to install the software. A system dialog box asking if you want to allow the program to make changes to the computer may appear. Click Yes to continue the installation process. You may be required to enter an Administrator password at this point.

The default installation directory is C:\Program Files (x86)\FAARFIELD2\. The installer will create this directory if it does not already exist. The installer will also create a new program group called FAARFIELD. The FAARFIELD 2.0 installation directory is separate from the FAARFIELD 1.42 version to avoid overwriting older files. Both versions can run on the same computer at the same time. FAARFIELD 2.0 will create a working directory in the user's My Documents folder, C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\, the first time the software is used. The working directory is the default location for storing job files and PDF report output. It also contains the traffic library, stored traffic patterns, UDA files, and various temporary files used during calculations and report generation.

Figure 3-1. FAARFIELD 2.0 Setup

title: Running the Program
html: FAARFIELD can be run from the start menu, desktop, or a job file. Once open, you may perform a design or analysis before exiting the software.

title: Opening from the Start Menu
html:
By default, the installer creates a Start Menu item called FAARFIELD2. To run the program from the Start Menu:

  1. Click the Windows Start button
  2. Locate FAARFIELD2 on the Windows Program Menu as shown in Figure 4-1.
  3. Click the FAARFIELD2 menu item to start the program.

Figure 4-1. FAARFIELD 2.0 in the Windows Start Button Menu

title: Opening from the Desktop
html:
The installer creates a shortcut icon on the desktop called FAARFIELD2 by default, as shown in Figure 4-2. Double click the FAARFIELD2 icon to start the program.

Figure 4-2. FAARFIELD 2.0 Windows Desktop Shortcut Icon

title: Opening from a Job File
html:
FAARFIELD 2.0 data are stored in job files having the extension *.jobx, as shown in Figure 4-3. The installer will associate these files with FAARFIELD by default. Once associated, any Windows "Open File" action, including double-clicking, select→press Enter, or right click→Open, will start FAARFIELD and open that job file.

Figure 4-3. Access FAARFIELD 2.0 by *.jobx Files

FAARFIELD 1.42 data are stored in job files having the extension *.JOB.xml, as shown in Figure 4-4. FAARFIELD 2.0 is capable of opening job files created by FAARFIELD 1.42, but the installer does not associate this extension with FAARFIELD by default because the final part of the extension, xml, is used for many different types of data by many different programs. Associating it with FAARFIELD could cause problems with other software on the host computer. To open FAARFIELD 2.0 from a FAARFIELD 1.42 file, right click the job file and then click Open with. Select More apps on the dialog shown in Figure 4-5 and choose FAARFIELD_MVVM then OK.

Figure 4-4. Access FAARFIELD 2.0 by *.JOB.xml Files

Figure 4-5. Starting FAARFIELD using Open with

Both *.jobx and *.JOB.xml job files can be associated with FAARFIELD 2.0 using the right click→Open with interface. Check the Always use this app to open .jobx files box to associate the files with FAARFIELD 2.0 and make it the default Open with application.

Additional information regarding job files can be found in Jobs and Job Files and in Appendix D: Data Files.

title: Performing a Design or Analysis
html:
FAARFIELD opens with an empty section as shown in Figure 4-6, similar to how a new word processing file opens with an empty document. The interface allows a user to input pavement structure data and section traffic, then perform various design or analysis calculations. The minimum required steps for performing a design or analysis are:

  1. Enter the pavement type.
  2. Enter the design traffic.
  3. Select the analysis type.
  4. Click the Run button.
  5. View the analysis results by selecting the appropriate report from the Explorer tab.

Steps 1, 2, and 3 may be performed in any order so long as all three steps are completed prior to step 4.

Figure 4-6. Default FAARFIELD Interface

title: Exit Software
html:
To close the FAARFIELD program, click Exit located on the upper left area of the toolbar or click the "X" in the upper right corner of the window frame. A dialogue box asks the user if they want to exit the program, as illustrated in Figure 4-7. Click Yes to exit and No to continue using the program.

Figure 4-7. Software Exit Dialog Box

title: Program Interface
html: The FAARFIELD interface uses sub-screens and tabs to display pavement design and analysis information in a user-configurable and easily understood format. The default display provides the section traffic data and structure data simultaneously in the center of the screen. The explorer interface on the left organizes sections and jobs, provides access to the vehicle library to add vehicles to the section traffic, and provides access to the material library to define pavement structure. Design options can be displayed on the right-hand side of the screen. A toolbar is provided at the top of the screen for commonly-used job file actions, use batch mode, and to create or edit User Defined Aircraft. The interface uses a docking system to allow users to customize the layout of the interface to suit their preferences.

title: Explorer Interface
html:
The Explorer, highlighted with a solid line in Figure 5-1, is a tabbed interface modeled after the tree-view of the Windows File Explorer. The Explorer tab lists open jobs and the sections within each job file, allowing the user to define and switch between multiple job files and sections at once. Right clicking on a job or section name will open a context menu to control jobs and sections, highlighted with a dashed line in Figure 5-1. Selecting the Traffic tab lists aircraft and vehicles in the Vehicle Library that can be added to the design traffic of a pavement section. The Material tab lists materials in the Material Library that can be added as a layer in a pavement section.

Figure 5-1. Explorer Interface with Right Click Context Menu

title: Interface Multi-Use Area
html:
The Multi-Use area is the top center portion of the program interface as shown in Figure 5-2. It displays pavement structure information when the program is first opened. This area also displays job and section details, analysis results and reports, and aircraft gear configurations. The contents of the Multi-Use area are controlled by the Explorer Interface and by the tabs at the top of the Multi-Use Area, highlighted in Figure 5-3.

Figure 5-2. Section Information Interface

Figure 5-3. Tabs at the Top of the Multi-Use Area

title: Section Traffic Interface
html:
The Section Traffic Interface is a grid listing the design aircraft of the current section and their properties. It is displayed at the bottom center of the interface by default, as shown in Figure 5-4.

Figure 5-4. Section Traffic Interface

title: Toolbar Interface
html:
The Toolbar is located at the top of the program screen. It is used to create and control jobs and sections, manage User Defined Aircraft, use batch mode, access this help file, and exit the program.

Figure 5-5. FAARFIELD Toolbar

title: Notes and Design Options Interface
html:
Notes and Design Options are pinned to the right-hand side of the program interface, as shown in Figure 5-6. Notes are displayed by default. Design Options are accessed from the Explorer interface.

Figure 5-6. Notes and Design Options Interface

title: Dock System
html:
FAARFIELD 2.0 uses a docking system that allows users to re-configure the interface to suit their preference. Each portion of the interface is implemented as an independent sub-screen that can be resized and moved around within the overall software interface, as shown in Figure 5-7. Supported actions include Float, Dock, Tab, Auto hide, Hide, Pin, and Resize. The Dock Action Menu is the main interface for the docking system. It is accessed by clicking the down-arrow on the upper-right hand corner of the sub-screens, as shown in Figure 5-8. Right clicking a tab in the Multi-Use area also accesses the Dock Action Menu. User-defined interface configurations are not saved at this time. The software will open with the default screen layout regardless of changes to the interface during previous use of FAARFIELD. The default configuration can also be restored by clicking the Reset button on the Toolbar.

A link to documentation for the docking system is provided for reference only and does not imply endorsement of a particular software library or product by the FAA.

Figure 5-7. Rearranged Sub-Screens

Figure 5-8. Sub-Screen Actions Accessed from Down Arrow Button or Right click of a Tab

title: Floated Sub-Screen
html:
Sub-screens can be "popped out" from the interface and placed in a separate window. This feature is accessed from the Floating menu item. The resulting window can be moved around the Windows Desktop independently from the rest of the program using standard Windows controls. The default location for a floated sub-screen is the upper left area of the program screen. The sub-screen can be resized and moved as needed. An example with the Traffic Interface sub-screen floated is shown in Figure 5-9.

Figure 5-9. Floated Traffic Sub-Screen

title: Tabbed Sub-Screen
html:
Selecting Tabbed document adds the sub-screen as a tab in the Multi-use area, as shown in Figure 5-10. Right clicking the tab will access the Dock Action Menu, as shown in Figure 5-11.

Figure 5-10. Sub-Screen Tabbed Document Action of Traffic Interface

Figure 5-11. Sub-Screen Action Accessed by Right Clicking Tab in Multi-Use Area

title: Dockable Sub-Screen
html:
Dockable sub-screens are anchored to one of nine positions within the interface. Interfaces are made dockable by selecting Dockable from the Dock Action Menu of an interface. Clicking and dragging a dockable sub-screen will cause the docking controls to appear, as shown in Figure 5-10. Dragging the sub-screen to the cross-shaped control in the middle of the screen will cause the window to dock in the current frame, as shown in Figure 5-13. Dragging the sub-screen to a control at the edge docks the sub-screen to the top-level frame of the application, as shown in Figure 5-14. Notice how the Explorer and Note interfaces were shortened to make room for the Traffic Interface in Figure 5-14, but in Figure 5-13 the Traffic Interface was made narrower to fit below the Multi-Use area.

Figure 5-12. Sub-Screen Docking Controls

Figure 5-13. Traffic Interface Docked to Current Frame

Figure 5-14. Traffic Interface Docked to Top-Level Frame of Application

title: Pinning and Auto-Hiding Docked Sub-Screens
html:
Sub-screens are either pinned to their locations within the docking system or unpinned into Auto Hide mode. The pin icon to highlighted in Figure 5-16 pins and unpins sub-screens within the interface. Pinned sub-screens are always visible. Unpinning a sub-screen is analogous to minimizing an application in Windows. The sub-screen is hidden, and tab with the name of the sub-screen is created at the nearest edge of the screen, as shown in Figure 5-15. Hovering or clicking on the tab will restore the sub-screen to its previous location. The interface will be hidden again as soon as the user clicks in a different sub-screen. Clicking the pin icon again while the sub-screen is visible will exit Auto Hide mode and pin the sub-screen to its location.

Figure 5-15. Interface After Traffic Sub-Screen Un-Pinned

Figure 5-16. Pin Icon

title: Hide (Close) Sub-Screen
html:
Sub-screens have a hide button (Close or X button) at the top right corner of their frames, highlighted in Figure 5-17. Sub-screens can also be hidden using the Hide sub-screen menu item highlighted in Figure 5-8. Hiding the screen removes it from the interface. Selecting the hidden interface in the Explorer will restore it to the Multi-Use area. Hidden sub-screens may also be restored with the Reset button or closing then re-opening the software. The Hide button is disabled on sub-screens not listed in the Explorer Interface, including the Traffic Interface, because it is not possible to restore them once closed.

Figure 5-17. Hide Button at Top Right of Sub-Screen

title: Reset Interface to Default
html: To return to the original default program screen arrangement of a section in a job file, click Reset on the upper left area of the Toolbar. For example, if screens in a section are moved or resized, clicking Reset can quickly return the program screen to the original layout.

title: Job and Section Definition and Control
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
FAARFIELD organizes data and calculations into jobs. A job consists of a group of related sections, with each section consisting of a structure, traffic pattern, and analysis type. Each job may contain multiple sections. There is no theoretical limit to the number of sections a job file may contain.

The Explorer controls which section of which job is currently displayed by the interface. Clicking a section in the Explorer makes it the current section, loading it into the Multi-Use area for manipulation by the user. The Toolbar contains the controls for creating, opening, saving, and closing job files, as well as the controls for creating new sections within a job.

title: Jobs and Job Files
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html: Each job is stored in a job file on the user's computer. FAARFIELD can open more than one job file simultaneously. Job files are normal files on the computer and can be moved, copied, or deleted just like any other file. FAARFIELD can be open a job file from any location, including removable media such as thumb drives. Job files contain all information pertinent to the analysis. A job file created on one computer can be opened and manipulated with FAARFIELD on another computer, similar to how a word processing file created on one computer can be opened on a different computer.

title: Creating New Jobs
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The New Job button on the Toolbar creates a blank new job with a single blank section in FAARFIELD. New jobs appear in and are managed with the Explorer Interface, as illustrated in Figure 6-1 that shows three new jobs in the Explorer. The job name is set by the user in the Section interface, as shown in Figure 6-2. The job file is not created on disk until the user saves the job. The job name is used for the job file name, and the Explorer interface is updated to reflect the new job name. Any character that is permitted in a file name by the underlying Windows operating system can be used in the job name. FAARFIELD 2.0 job files have the extension *.jobx and are stored as XML. The default location for storing job files is the FAARFIELD working directory C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\, but the user can store a job file anywhere in the user's file system. FAARFIELD 2.0 will open multiple job files at one time.

Figure 6-1. Job List in Explorer Interface

Figure 6-2. Job Name Set in Section Interface

title: Opening Existing Jobs
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The Open Job button of the Toolbar launches the Windows Open dialog box for the user to locate and open a job file in FAARFIELD. The default location for job files is the FAARFIELD working directory C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD, as shown in Figure 6-3. The newly opened job is listed in the Explorer Interface, as shown in Figure 6-4. The Multi-Use area shows the details of the job.

FAARFIELD 2.0 can open FAARFIELD 1.42 job files in read-only mode. The default FAARFIELD 1.42 job file location is C:\...\Documents\FAARFIELD. They have the extension *.job.xml, as shown in Figure 6-5. The Multi-Use area has a red border when working with a FAARFIELD 1.42 job file, as shown in Figure 6-6. FAARFIELD 2.0 will not save changes in the FAARFIELD 1.42 format; it will create a *.jobx file in FAARFIELD 2.0 format if the user attempts to save a FAARFIELD 1.42 file.

Figure 6-3. Windows Open Dialog Box

Figure 6-4. Opened Job Listed in Explorer Interface

Figure 6-5. Opening an FAARFIELD 1.42 Job File

Figure 6-6. FAARFIELD 1.42 Files Have a Red Border When Opened in FAARFIELD 2.0

title: Pavement Sections in a Job
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
Each job contains one or more sections. A section consists of a pavement structure, traffic pattern, and analysis type. Sections are defined by the needs of the user. They can represent different pieces of pavement, such as runway keel and edge sections, or represent alternative designs for the same piece of pavement, such as when comparing an asphalt pavement design to a concrete pavement design for a rehabilitation project. Users can name jobs and sections in the Section Interface or Job Information form. The name will be synchronized and displayed in the Explorer Interface.

FAARFIELD opens with blank job containing a single blank section, however, job files may contain more than one section. The software provides two methods for adding sections to jobs: creation of a new blank section using the Toolbar and copy/paste of an existing section from the right click menu of the Explorer. The delete section function is also on the right-click context menu of the Explorer.

title: New Section
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The New Section button on the Toolbar creates a new blank section in the current job. The new section is appended to the job. The default section name is "New Section 1".

Figure 6-7. New Section Button on Toolbar

title: Copy, Paste, or Delete a Section
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
Sections can be copied and pasted to create a duplicate of a section, or they can be copied from one job and pasted into another job.

To copy a section, right click the section name to access the context menu, as shown in Figure 6-8, then click Copy.

To paste a section, first copy a section. Then right click on a section in the job to which the section will be pasted and select Paste from the context menu. FAARFIELD will append "Copy" to the section name and add the copied section to the job.

The Delete item of right-click menu will delete all data for the section and remove it from the job file. Delete is irreversible.

Figure 6-8. Right Click Context Menu to Copy, Delete, or Paste a Section in Explorer

title: Saving Jobs
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html: The user can save a job to disk in a job file at any time except when a design or analysis is running (the Run button has been pressed and a long-running calculation is in progress). FAARFIELD saves all information in a job file at the same time; users cannot save one pavement section but not another within the same job file. FAARFIELD provides three buttons on the Toolbar for saving jobs: Save Job, Save As, and Save All.

title: Save Job
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html: The Save Job button on the Toolbar saves the current job to disk. If the job has not been saved before, FAARFIELD will launch the Save As dialog to ask the user where to save the job file. FAARFIELD saves all sections in the job file; sections cannot be saved individually.

title: Save As
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The Save As button on the Toolbar saves the current job file to location specified by the user. A dialog box will appear requesting the user to enter a new name and location for the new job file. FAARFIELD uses the standard Windows Save As dialog, shown in Figure 6-9. Clicking Cancel will close the dialog box without creating a new job file. The default location for saving a job is the FAARFIELD working directory (C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD).

Figure 6-9. Save As Dialog Box

title: Save All
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html: The Save All button on the Toolbar performs the Save Job function for all open FAARFIELD jobs.

title: Closing Jobs
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
To close a job, select the job to be closed by clicking the job name in the Explorer then click Close Job on the Toolbar. Alternatively, right-click on the job name and select Close Job from the context menu. If the job has been changed since the last time it was saved, a dialogue box asks the user if they want to save the job file, as shown in Figure 6-10. Click Yes to save the job file then close it. Click No to close the job file and message box without saving the file. Closing a job without saving will cause all unsaved data in that job file to be lost. Closed jobs are no longer displayed in the Explorer. Clicking Cancel will leave the job open.

Figure 6-10. Job Closing Dialog Box

title: Job Information
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The Job Information item in the Explorer opens the Job Information form illustrated in Figure 6-11 in the Multi-Use area. This form provides a place to record information about the job, such as the location, designer, AIP information, or general comments. FAARFIELD stores values for Frost depth, Surface Drainage, and Frost Design Method, but does not use them during design calculations. FAARFIELD also allows network, branch, and section identifiers from a pavement management section to be stored as part of the job information.

Figure 6-11. Job Information Window

title: Selecting Mode of Operation
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
FAARFIELD supports four design and analysis modes: Design, Life, Life and Compaction, and ACR/PCR. The drop-down box highlighted in Figure 6-12 sets the mode of operation for each section. Each section in a job can have a different mode. Sections may have only one mode at a time, however it is possible change modes between runs. The default mode is Thickness Design.

Figure 6-12. Mode of Operation

title: Run/Cancel
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The Run button, highlighted in Figure 6-13, executes the selected analysis on the current section. If batch mode is enabled, the Run button starts computations for the selected sections. Once the design or analysis process starts, the Run button is replaced by Cancel so the user can interrupt a long-running analysis they do not wish to complete. Note that the Cancel button will not interrupt FAASR3D calculations and FAARFIELD must wait for FAASR3D to complete the current iteration before cancelling the process. It may be several minutes before the analysis is cancelled.

FAARFIELD supports running multiple instances at the same time, however, only one design/analysis calculation may be active. Users cannot start two copies of FAARFIELD and press Run in both copies.

Figure 6-13. Run Button

title: Batch Mode
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
FAARFIELD provides a batch option to execute multiple designs and analyses with a single click of the Run button. This is useful for performing several calculations while the software is unattended, for example, executing several long-running computations overnight. Each pavement section has an Add to Batch option, highlighted in Figure 6-14. Enabling this option for one or more sections puts FAARFIELD into batch mode. A single batch mode run may contain sections with different modes of operation (design, life, compaction, or PCR). When the Run button is pressed, FAARFIELD will perform computations for each section sequentially. Computations will not be performed for sections with the Add to Batch option disabled. Note that if the current section has Add to Batch disabled but other sections have it enabled, FAARFIELD will not perform computations for the current section, it will perform computations only for those sections with the option enabled. The Deselect All button on the Toolbar will disable Add to Batch for all open sections and return FAARFIELD to its normal operating mode, where the Run button performs computations for the current section. The Select All button on the Toolbar will enable Add to Batch for all open sections.

Figure 6-14. Add To Batch Option for a Section

title: Include in Summary Report
group: Job and Section Definition and Control
html:
The Include in Summary Report checkbox, highlighted in Figure 6-15, includes the section in the Summary Report.

Figure 6-15. Include in Summary Report Checkbox

title: Defining Pavement Structure
html:
FAARFIELD works by comparing the capacity of a pavement structure to the demand placed on the pavement section by a traffic mix. Pavement structure is the set of material thicknesses and properties of a pavement section. Pavement structure is defined using the Section tab of the Multi-Use area, shown in Figure 7-1. Defining pavement structure requires setting the pavement structure type, modifying the pavement layers using the grid or image, then setting the general pavement properties and mode-specific parameters of the pavement.

Figure 7-1. Pavement Structure Interface

FAARFIELD includes a library of layer materials for customizing pavement structures. For rigid pavements, the minimum number of layers is two and the maximum is five layers. For flexible pavements, the minimum number of layers is two with no maximum. Some of the layer types can be placed at any position in a structure, while others can only be placed in specified positions. FAARFIELD will provide a warning if the user attempts to place a layer in a position that is not allowed. FAARFIELD determines automatically which design procedure to execute based on the layers in the pavement structure. Most layer types correspond to FAA specification items found in AC 150/5370-10, and the user's ability to adjust the properties of these standard materials is very limited. Some flexibility is allowed by the inclusion of the User Defined layer type. However, the User-Defined layer type does not meet FAA standards for airport pavement design.

title: General Pavement Structure Properties
html: General pavement structure properties are those that pertain to the whole structure, not individual layers in the structure. These are the pavement type, design life, and design layer. FAARFIELD calculates two additional properties, the calculated pavement life and total thickness of the pavement.

title: Pavement Type
html:
Pavement is set with the drop-down box highlighted in Figure 7-2. FAARFIELD supports six types of pavement structures: New Flexible, HMA on Aggregate, HMA on Flexible, HMA on Rigid, New Rigid, PCC on Flexible, and Unbonded on Rigid. Selecting a pavement type deletes any existing layer information for the section and loads the default layer thicknesses and properties for that type into the grid and image. The pavement type determines the design procedure FAARFIELD uses for design and analysis.

Figure 7-2. Pavement Type Selection

title: New Flexible
html:
New Flexible is the default pavement type. It consists of HMA surface, an HMA stabilized base, and a high-quality granular subbase layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-3. FAARFIELD uses a flexible design procedure for New Flexible pavement sections.

Figure 7-3. Default New Flexible Layers

title: HMA on Aggregate
html:
The HMA on Aggregate pavement type consists of an HMA surface, granular base, and granular subbase. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-4. FAARFIELD uses a flexible design procedure for HMA on Aggregate pavement sections.

Figure 7-4. Default HMA on Aggregate Layers

title: HMA on Flexible
html:
The HMA on Flexible pavement type consists of HMA Overlay, HMA surface, flexible variable base, and high-quality granular subbase layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-5. FAARFIELD uses a flexible design procedure for HMA on Aggregate pavement sections.

Figure 7-5. Default HMA on Flexible Layers

title: HMA on Rigid
html:
The HMA on Rigid pavement type consists of HMA overlay, PCC surface layer, HMA stabilized base, and high-quality granular subbase layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-6. FAARFIELD uses an HMA Overlay on Rigid Pavement design procedure for HMA on Rigid pavement sections.

Figure 7-6. Default HMA on Rigid Layers

title: New Rigid
html:
The New Rigid pavement type consists of PCC surface, HMA Stabilized base, and high-quality granular subbase layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-7. FAARFIELD uses a rigid pavement design procedure for New Rigid pavement sections.

Figure 7-7. Default New Rigid Layers

title: PCC on Flexible
html:
The PCC on Flexible pavement type consists of a PCC overlay, HMA surface, and high-quality granular base layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-8. FAARFIELD uses the new rigid pavement design procedure for PCC on Flexible pavement sections.

Figure 7-8. Default PCC on Flexible Layers

title: Unbonded on Rigid
html:
The Unbonded on Rigid pavement type consists of PCC overlay, PCC surface, rigid variable, and high-quality granular subbase layers. The default layers are shown in Figure 7-9. FAARFIELD uses the rigid overlay design procedure for PCC on Flexible pavement sections. A partially-bonded design procedure can be accessed if the Partially Bonded Overlay on Rigid option is set to Yes in Design Options. FAA considers a partially-bonded overlay a non-standard design.

Figure 7-9. Default Unbonded on Rigid Layers

title: Design Life
html:
The Design Life is the expected pavement life, in years, for a pavement thickness design. It is used by the design procedure to determine the expected traffic volume over the life of the pavement. It is an input to the design procedure and is distinct from the Calculated Life that is an output of FAARFIELD. Design life can be assigned a value within the range of 1 to 50 years. The standard design life is 20 years, as shown in Figure 7-10. A warning is displayed if a non-standard design life is used, but design and analysis computations are permitted.

Figure 7-10. Design Life Input

title: Design Layer
html:
The Design Layer is the layer in the pavement structure that FAARFIELD varies during the design procedure. It is set from the grid interface by clicking a layer in the grid then then the Select As The Design Layer button. The current design layer has a red arrow indicator in the grid interface and a green outline in the image interface, as shown in Figure 7-11.

Figure 7-11. Set as the Design Layer Button

title: Calculated Life
html:
The Calculated Life is FAARFIELD's estimate of how long a pavement structure will last when subjected to traffic. Calculated Life is based on CDF concepts and determined using the design procedure. Calculated life is shown only after calculations in Life or Life and Compaction modes, as shown in Figure 7-12. It is blank in Pavement Design and PCR modes.

Figure 7-12. Calculated Life Display

title: Total Thickness to the Top of the Subgrade
html:
The Total thickness to the top of the subgrade displays the total layer thickness of the pavement structure, as shown in Figure 7-13. It is equal to the sum of the thicknesses of all non-subgrade layers.

Figure 7-13. Total Thickness Display

title: Mode-Specific Pavement Structure Parameters
html:
FAARFIELD accepts two inputs specific to overlay of rigid pavements: Cumulative Damage Factor Used and Structural Condition Index. Input boxes for these are visible only when the pavement type is HMA on Rigid or Unbonded on Rigid, as shown in Figure 7-14.

Figure 7-14. Mode-Specific Input Boxes

title: Structural Condition Index (SCI)
html:
Overlaid rigid pavement (HMA on Rigid and Unbonded on Rigid) designs require an input value for the Structural Condition Index (SCI) for the existing pavement. SCI is a rigid pavement condition index derived from the Pavement Condition Index (PCI), in which only certain distress types associated with load-related damage are considered. It is entered in the SCI box highlighted in Figure 7-16. It is a mode-specific parameter and the input box is not visible except when the pavement type is HMA on Rigid or Unbonded on Rigid.

Figure 7-15. SCI Input Box

SCI is derived from PCI and thus is based on a visual survey of the pavement surface, following ASTM D5340, "Standard Test Method for Airport Pavement Condition Index Surveys." The specific distresses included in the SCI are: Corner Breaks; Longitudinal/Transverse/Diagonal Cracks; Corner Spalls; Edge Spalls; and Shattered Slabs. The distress type "low-severity shrinkage cracks" is also considered in evaluating SCI, but only to describe early structural cracks that have not yet progressed to full width or depth. Because SCI includes only some of the distress types used to compute PCI, the value of SCI will always be equal to or higher than the PCI for the same pavement evaluation.

In previous FAA overlay design methods (most recently, cancelled AC 150/5320-6E), the condition of existing PCC pavements receiving overlays was quantified using factors cb and cr. While these factors are no longer used, in some cases it may be possible to estimate the SCI of the receiving pavement given an available value of cb or cr.

For a concrete overlay on rigid pavement, SCI can be estimated from the following equation:

For an asphalt overlay on rigid pavements, SCI can be estimated from the following equation:

SCI=100cb-25; 0.75≤ cb ≤1

Both equations are from Rollings, R.S., Design of Overlays for Rigid Airport Pavements, Report No. DOT/FAA/PM-87/19, April 1988. Note that the relationship is not valid when SCI is between 75 and 100.

title: Cumulative Damage Factor Used (CDFU)
html:
The Cumulative Damage Factor Used (CDFU) for an existing pavement is related to the remaining life of that pavement. It is entered in the Percent CDFU box highlighted in Figure 7-16. It is a mode-specific parameter and the input box is not visible except when the pavement type is HMA on Rigid or Unbonded on Rigid.

Figure 7-16. CDFU Input Box

When the Structural Condition Index equals 100 for overlay design of an existing rigid pavement, an additional input is required to define the amount of life that has been used by the existing pavement up to the time of the overlay. The input is in terms of "CDF used to first crack" (CDFU) (Rollings, R.S., Design of Overlays for Rigid Airport Pavements, Report No. DOT/FAA/PM-87/19, April 1988. P. 98, eq. 42). For aggregate base layers only, and assuming that traffic on the pavement has been constant over time, a good estimate of CDFU can be obtained from:

LU = number of years of operation of the existing pavement until overlay

LD = design life of the existing pavement in years

In general, this relationship is not valid for rigid pavements on high quality, stabilized bases. For such structures, it is recommended that the FAARFIELD Life function be used to compute CDFU based on an estimate of traffic applied to the pavement up to the time of overlay.

The procedure for computing percent CDFU for a rigid pavement with SCI = 100 is as follows:

  1. Set up the structure based on the original design assumptions.
  2. Estimate the traffic applied to the original pavement up to the time of overlay and add to the airplane design list.
  3. Set design life to the amount of time the pavement will have been in operation up to the time of overlay.
  4. Run in Life mode.

Percent CDFU will be displayed when the computation is completed. If the above procedure produces a value of percent CDFU greater than 100, then enter 100 for percent CDFU for the overlay design. If it is suspected that the pavement has been subjected to more, or heavier, traffic than assumed in the Life mode, percent CDFU should be increased from the computed value. In general, setting percent CDFU to 100 will result in the most conservative design.

For PCC-on-rigid overlays, FAARFIELD varies the modulus of the base pavement as a function of SCI. The reduced modulus computation is automatic and transparent to the user.

title: P/TC Ratio
html: FAARFIELD considers only departures and ignores arrival traffic due to its significantly lower weight, so a standard traffic cycle (TC) includes one takeoff and one landing of the same airplane. One traffic cycle produces one pass of the airplane which results in a pass-to-traffic cycle ratio (P/TC) of 1. To determine annual departures for pavement design purposes, multiply the number of departing airplanes by the P/TC ratio. For most airport pavement design purposes, a P/TC of 1 may be used. In cases where the landing weight is not significantly low or in a case where the airplane must travel along the pavement more than once, it may be appropriate to adjust and increase the pass-to-traffic cycle (P/TC) ratio to more than 1. Additional details can be found in AC 150/5335-5, "Standardized Method of Reporting Airport Pavement Strength – PCN," Appendix 1.

title: Material Library
html:
The Material Library is accessed from the Material tab of the Explorer Interface, as shown in Figure 7-17. It lists the materials available for defining a pavement structure in FAARFIELD. The materials are grouped into types: General, Aggregate, P-401/P-403 HMA, P-501 PCC, and Stabilized.

Figure 7-17. Material Library Tab in Explorer Interface

All layer types (except User-Defined) correspond to materials referenced in AC 150/5320-6. This section provides information on the relationships between the FAARFIELD layer types and AC 150/5320-6, and provides additional guidance on selecting appropriate layer properties as input data for FAARFIELD.

The requirements and guidelines of AC 150/5320-6 should be followed whenever there is a discrepancy between FAARFIELD and the advisory circular. For example, minimum allowable thicknesses for layers have been built into FAARFIELD to conform to the applicable requirements of AC 150/5320-6. However, minimum thicknesses from FAARFIELD should always be checked against the requirements of the advisory circular for the particular pavement type under design to ensure that the design meets the current standards.

title: General Layers
html: The general layers consist of the Subgrade Layer and the User Defined Layer.

title: Subgrade Layer
html:
The subgrade layer is the lowest layer in the pavement structure unless the Alternate Subgrade design option is enabled. The thickness of the subgrade layer is assumed to be infinite and cannot be assigned a value. Subgrade modulus values for flexible pavement design can be determined by the user for input into FAARFIELD in a number of ways. The procedure that is applicable in most cases is to use available CBR values and substitute the relationship:

E = 1,500 × CBR (E in psi)

This method provides designs compatible with earlier flexible design procedures based on subgrade CBR. Although FAARFIELD performs computations based on elastic modulus, direct input of CBR values is also acceptable.

Similarly, for rigid pavement design, the foundation modulus can be expressed as the modulus of subgrade reaction k or as the elastic (Young's) modulus E and can be input into the program directly in either form. However, all structural computations are performed using the elastic modulus E. If the foundation modulus is input as a k-value it is automatically converted to the equivalent E value using the following equations (which are equivalent):

k =0.09643× ESG0.7788

or,

ESG=20.15×k1.284

where:

ESG

= Elastic (Young's) modulus of the subgrade, psi

k

= Modulus of Subgrade Reaction, pci

The above conversion formulas are described in the following reference:

Tuleubekov, K., and Brill, D.R., Correlation between Subgrade Reaction Modulus and CBR for Airport Pavement Subgrades, ASCE, Second Transportation & Development Congress 2014, Orlando, Florida, June 8-11, 2014.

For existing pavement the E modulus can be determined in the field from non-destructive testing (NDT) such as falling-weight deflectometer (FWD) testing. This may be necessary if direct testing of the subgrade is impractical. If the subgrade is accessible then the k-value can be determined directly by plate-load testing. If the k-modulus can be determined by plate load testing, or is otherwise available, then the k-value should be input directly into the FAARFIELD program without first converting to E modulus.

In cases where CBR data are available, an approximate conversion from CBR to k-value for the subgrade is:

k=28.6926× CBR0.7788(k in pci)

The equations for converting CBR and k to E modulus are based on empirical data and were used in the development of the flexible and rigid pavement failure models. Although the above linear conversion between CBR and elastic modulus is a common and useful design assumption used in airport pavement design, it is not theoretically correct. Correlations of CBR and elastic modulus for various subgrade materials show a great deal of scatter. Thus, it is recommended that the conversion equations above be used with caution.

For flexible pavements, this allows the user to produce alternate designs with asphalt modulus values different than the fixed standard value of 200,000 psi. Structures substituting user-defined layers for P-401 or P-403 do not meet FAA standards for airport pavement design; however, they may be useful for evaluating existing pavements with non-standard asphalt or for evaluating the effect of different material properties with the FAA design model. title: Aggregate Layers
html:
Aggregate layers in FAARFIELD correspond to one of the following FAA specification items: Item P-154, Subbase Course, Item P-209, Crushed Aggregate Base Course, Item P-208, Aggregate Base Course, or Item P-211, Lime Rock Base Course.

The modulus of crushed aggregate layers is computed automatically and cannot be changed manually. The internal modulus assignment procedure in FAARFIELD is based on sublayering of thick aggregate layers. The modulus of a given sublayer depends on the thickness of the sublayer, and also on the modulus of the layer immediately beneath it. Thus, within a given layer consisting of multiple sublayers, the higher sublayers are assigned higher modulus values than the lower sublayers. The thickness of sublayers is determined by the layer type. For uncrushed aggregate (P-154), the basic sublayer thickness is 8 inches, although the thickness of the top sublayer varies between 4 and 12 inches. For uncrushed aggregate layers 8 inches or less, or crushed aggregate layers 10 inches or less, no sublayering is performed. Modulus is assigned to the top layer as a function of thickness in such a way as to maintain a continuous functional relationship between modulus and layer thickness, even at "crossover" points where the number of sublayers increases or decreases by one. For crushed aggregate (e.g., P-209), the basic sublayer thickness is 10 inches, and the top sublayer varies between 5 and 15 inches thick. A detailed explanation of modulus determination for aggregate layers is provided in Appendix C.

Note: Sublayering of aggregate layers is not performed for rigid pavement designs that use the finite element analysis model. This is because additional layers of elements would increase the finite element solution time significantly. Instead, the modulus values that otherwise would be assigned to sublayers are computed using the algorithm described above. The average of the sublayer modulus values is assigned to a single layer of elements and displayed on the screen.

Aggregate layers can be placed anywhere in the pavement structure except at the top or bottom. The following additional restrictions also apply:

  1. Only one crushed layer and one uncrushed layer may be present in a structure. The maximum number of aggregate layers which may be present in a structure is two, one of each type.
  2. If crushed and uncrushed layers are adjacent, the crushed layer must be above the uncrushed layer.

For efficiency in iterating to a valid thickness design, a two-stage process is used during design with thick aggregate layers. When the CDF is outside the range of 0.5 to 2.0, the aggregate layers are not sublayered for LEAF, but are treated as a single layer with a modulus equal to the average of what would otherwise be the sublayer moduli. When CDF is within the range of 0.5 to 2.0, full sublayering is performed. One consequence of this is that the CDF can temporarily increase when sublayering first occurs. This is not an indication of an error in the procedure.

The modulus value displayed in the structure table for an aggregate layer is the average value of the sublayer modulus values. The only exception is for newly created layers, in which case the "default" values of 75,000 psi and 40,000 psi are displayed for crushed and uncrushed aggregate materials respectively. These defaults are never used in calculations.

title: P-154 Aggregate Subbase Layer
html: Item P-154 is an uncrushed aggregate material suitable for use as a subbase.

title: P-208 Uncrushed Aggregate Layer
html: Item P-208 is an uncrushed aggregate material suitable for use as a base or subbase. Note that the use of Item P-208 as a base material is limited by AC 150/5320-6 to pavements designed for gross loads of 60,000 lbs. (27,000 kg) or less. Accordingly, if P-208 is used as a base material and airplane in the traffic list exceeds 60,000 lbs., a message will be displayed, "Non-Standard Structure." Item P-208 can be used as a subbase layer without restriction.

title: P-209 Crushed Aggregate Layer
html: Item P-209 is a crushed aggregate material consisting of crushed natural aggregates. It suitable for use as a base or high-quality subbase.

title: P-211 Lime Rock Aggregate Layer
html: Item P-211 is a crushed aggregate material consisting of crushed lime rock aggregates. It is suitable for use as a base or high-quality subbase.

title: P-219 Recycled Concrete Aggregate Layer
html: Item P-219 is a crushed aggregate material consisting of crushed concrete pavement. It suitable for use as a base or high-quality subbase.

title: P-401/P-403 Hot Mix Asphalt Layers
html: Two types of hot mix asphalt (HMA) layers are available: HMA surface and HMA Overlay. Both types have the same properties, with modulus fixed at 200,000 psi and Poisson's ratio fixed at 0.35. For HMA used as a stabilized base layer, see the Stabilized Layer section.

title: P-401/P-403 Hot Mix Asphalt Surface Layer
html: Item P-401/P-403 Hot Mix Asphalt Surface Layer is a Hot Mix Asphalt material. The asphalt surface layer type can only be placed on the top of a structure, or under an HMA or PCC overlay.

title: P-401/P-403 Hot Mix Asphalt Overlay Layer
html: Item P-401/P-403 Hot Mix Asphalt Overlay Layer is a Hot Mix Asphalt material. The HMA asphalt overlay type can be placed over asphalt surface or PCC surface types.

title: P-501 Portland Cement Concrete Layers
html:
Three types of concrete layers are available: P-501 PCC Surface Layer, P-501 PCC Overlay (unbonded), and P-501 PCC Overlay on Flexible. The PCC surface type can be placed on the top of the structure for new designs or immediately below an overlay. The PCC overlay types can only be placed at the top of the structure. PCC overlay on flexible pavement can be placed on an asphalt layer or on a user defined layer.

The modulus of all PCC types is fixed at 4,000,000 psi except for a PCC surface when it is part of an overlay structure. Poisson's ratio is fixed at 0.15 in all cases. Flexural strength values can vary in the range from 500 to 1000 psi. (PCC modulus is considered to be independent of flexural strength.)

Overlaid rigid pavement designs require an input Structural Condition Index (SCI) value for the existing pavement. For unbonded overlays, it is assumed that the existing pavement may have suffered serious deterioration before the overlay and SCI values range from 100 (none to negligible structural cracking) to 67. For overlays on existing PCC with SCI=100 see Cumulative Damage Factor Used (CDFU).

For partially bonded overlays, it is assumed that the existing pavement is in sound to barely failed condition before the overlay and SCI values range from 100 (none to negligible cracking) to 67 (worse than the FAARFIELD definition of end-of-design-life of SCI = 80). Note that partially bonded overlays are no longer considered a standard FAA design in AC 150/5320-6. By default, this option is inactive in FAARFIELD; it can be activated from Design Options. However, if a partially bonded overlay is selected the following message will display: "Non-Standard Structure."

title: P-501 PCC Surface Layer
html: Item P-501 PCC Surface Layer is a Portland Cement Concrete layer. It can be placed at the surface of a pavement or beneath an overlay.

title: P-501 PCC Overlay (unbonded)
html: Item P-501 PCC Overlay (unbonded) is a Portland Cement Concrete layer. It can be placed at the surface of a pavement over a rigid layer.

title: P-501 PCC Overlay on Flexible
html: Item P-501 PCC Overlay on Flexible is a Portland Cement Concrete layer. It can be placed at the surface of a pavement over a flexible layer.

title: Editing Layers in a Pavement Structure with the Grid Interface
html:
The pavement grid is one of two main interfaces for defining and modifying pavement structures, the other being the image interface. The pavement grid interface is highlighted in Figure 7-18. The current structure shown in the grid and in the image are synchronized, with changes in one being immediately reflected in the other. It allows the user to add or remove layers from the structure, set the current design layer, and modify layer properties including thickness, Young's modulus, CBR (flexible pavements only), k (rigid pavements only), and modulus of rupture (PCC pavements only) as appropriate. Non-editable values in the grid are grayed out. An arrow located in the left column of the pavement grid indicates the current design layer.

Figure 7-18. Pavement Grid

Layers are added to the structure by dragging them from the Material Library and dropping them on the grid, as shown in Figure 7-19. Note that the user must first choose a pavement type before using the drag-and-drop function to add layer materials. The pavement type will be updated based on the drag-and-drop, e.g., by dragging a PCC overlay onto a flexible pavement structure will change the pavement type to PCC on Flexible. The Delete Selected Layer button highlighted in Figure 7-20 removes the currently selected layer from the pavement structure.

Figure 7-19. Drag and Drop from Material Library to Grid

Figure 7-20. Delete Selected Layer Button

title: Editing Layers in a Pavement Structure with the Image Interface
html:
FAARFIELD shows a cross section of the current structure in an image on the Structure tab in the Multi-Use area, as illustrated in Figure 7-21. FAARFIELD allows editing the pavement structure by double clicking a layer in the image. The structure shown in the grid and in the image are synchronized, with changes in one being immediately reflected in the other. Layers may be added, removed, or changed from the image and their properties may be edited, but the design layer must be set from the grid interface. The image can be copied to the clipboard and then pasted by clicking the Copy Structure to Clipboard button below the image.

Figure 7-21. Structure Window

title: Change a Layer Thickness, Modulus, or Strength Using the Image
html:
Click a layer in the pavement structure image to access the layer editing dialog. Figure 7-22 highlights the location of material properties in the dialog box. Edit the thickness, modulus of rupture, and modulus values and click OK to accept the changes or Cancel to revert to the previous values. Non-editable values are grayed out, e.g., subgrade thickness or modulus of P-401 (which has a fixed modulus value). Changing one of the modulus, CBR, or k values will automatically update the other two values.

Figure 7-22. Layer Properties in the Layer Editing Dialog Box

title: Add, Remove, or Change a Layer Material Using the Image
html:
Click a layer in the pavement structure image to access the layer editing dialog. Figure 7-23 highlights the material selection area in the dialog box. Select the desired material type and edit the layer properties, if desired. The Add Layer Below button inserts the layer of the selected material into the structure below the layer that was clicked in the image. The Add Layer Above button inserts a layer of the selected material into the structure above the layer that was clicked in the image. The OK button replaces the layer that was clicked in the image with a layer of the selected material. The Delete Layer button removes the layer that was clicked in the image from the pavement structure. The Cancel button closes the layer editing dialog without making any changes to the pavement structure.

Figure 7-23. Materials Selection in the Layer Editing Dialog Box

title: Defining Section Traffic Mix
html:
FAARFIELD works by comparing the capacity of a pavement structure to the demand placed on the pavement section by a traffic mix. The traffic mix is the list of vehicles that use (or are expected to use) the pavement section. Each pavement section has its own traffic mix. The traffic mix is defined using the vehicle library portion of the Explorer and the traffic interface, both highlighted in Figure 8-1.

Figure 8-1. Vehicle Library and Traffic Interface

title: Vehicle Library
html:
FAARFIELD contains a library of vehicles that can be used for design and analysis. The Aircraft tab of the Explorer, highlighted in Figure 8-2, accesses the vehicle library.

The vehicle library contains aircraft that are representative of the most common commercial and military airplanes. It also includes non-aircraft vehicles such as fuel trucks and emergency vehicles. Substitutions can be made for airplanes that are not included in the list by choosing a similar airplane or from the Generic group list. Data for the Generic group are based on generic airplane types used to generate design nomographs in previous FAA ACs. Alternatively, advanced users can add custom aircraft types using the User Defined Aircraft feature of FAARFIELD.

Vehicles are selected from the library and placed in the list of design vehicles, also referred to as the traffic mix, for a section. Except for gross load, annual departures, and percent annual growth, all necessary airplane information for design is stored internally as part of the library and cannot be changed by the user. The library itself is a cryptographically signed xml file stored in the user's working directory. If FAARFIELD detects a change to the library, all output from the program will include a "non-standard design" warning.

Figure 8-2. Aircraft Tab of Explorer Interface Accesses the Vehicle Library

The vehicle library is a set of linked windows listing the available vehicles including User Defined Aircraft, as shown in the Figure 8-3. Aircraft are organized into categories to make them easier to find in the library. The upper window named FAARFIELD Aircraft Group lists the categories of vehicles. User Defined Aircraft are listed in the External Library category. Clicking a category in the upper window shows the vehicles in that category in the lower window called FAARFIELD Aircraft Library. Double clicking a vehicle adds it to the traffic mix for the current section. Vehicles can also be added to the traffic mix by dragging-and-dropping a vehicle from the library to the traffic grid.

Figure 8-3. Vehicle Library

title: Traffic for the Current Section
html:
The traffic mix for the current section is shown in the traffic interface, highlighted in Figure 8-4. The interface is a grid containing the list of vehicles that use a pavement section, their weight, number of departures, and annual growth of the number of departures. It also displays the CDF contribution of each aircraft and the read-only vehicle parameters stored in the vehicle library. If Compute ACR for All Subgrade Categories is selected in the Design Options, the traffic interface will display the ACR value of each vehicle for each subgrade category. The traffic interface has features to store and recall traffic mixes for use on multiple sections.

Figure 8-4. Traffic Interface

title: Add Traffic to the Current Section
html:
Vehicles are added to the traffic mix for the current section by double clicking the vehicle in the vehicle library, or by drag-and-drop from the vehicle library to the grid of the traffic interface. Vehicles are added to the traffic mix with default values stored in the vehicle library. Users should edit the Gross Taxi Weight, Annual Departures, and Annual Growth traffic parameters to reflect their actual or expected values for each vehicle.

Airplanes with complex landing gear assemblies consisting of separate wing and belly gears are treated in design as two separate vehicles: a wing gear airplane and a belly gear airplane. Although the wing and belly gear airplanes appear as two separate lines in the aircraft list, they are linked together and can only be added or removed as a pair. The data for both airplanes is also linked, so changing the data for either one automatically changes the data for the other. Airplanes in which this applies include the following types: 2D/2D2 (such as B747 series); 2D/3D2 (such as A380 series); 2D/D1 (such as DC10-30/40, MD-11, and A340-200/300), and 2D/2D1 (such as A340-500/600).

The remaining parameters are read only, with values provided either from the vehicle library or from FAARFIELD calculations. In the column headings, P/C refers to pass/coverage, GW is short for gross weight, and ACR is aircraft classification rating (ACR).

The fraction of the gross weight carried by the main gear is set at 95 percent for all airplanes in the vehicle library to comply with the requirements of AC 150/5320-6. Tire Contact Lengths and Tire Contact Widths are used in the calculation of P/C Ratio. For this purpose, an elliptical contact patch is assumed, with its area equal to the tire load divided by the tire pressure. title: Gross Weight
html: Gross weight is the total weight of the entire vehicle, including passengers, cargo, and fuel.

title: Annual Departures
html: The value displayed in the Annual Departures field is defined as the number of annual departures for the selected vehicle at the start of the pavement's design life, that is, before any annual growth has been applied.

title: Annual Growth
html: Percent annual growth is defined as the percent change in annual departures per year over the design life of the pavement. Negative values represent a decrease in annual departures. Large negative percent annual growth can result in negative airplane departures before the end of the design life has been reached. The program automatically detects this condition if it occurs and assumes zero departures for the airplane from the time at which the departure rate becomes zero to the end of the design life.

title: User Defined Aircraft
html: FAARFIELD has an internal vehicle library containing most of the common aircraft in commercial service. Occasionally, it may be necessary to include vehicles in the traffic mix that do not appear in the internal library. FAARFIELD allows users to define and edit vehicles from the user interface. These user-defined aircraft (UDA) are treated just like internal library vehicles in the design. They are identified by suffix "(UDA)" following the aircraft name in all FAARFIELD reports. They appear in the External Library category of the vehicle library.

title: Creating a User Defined Aircraft
html:
The following example shows how to create a UDA in FAARFIELD. Consider the flexible pavement design example shown in Figure 8-11. To add a UDA to the current traffic mix, click the Create New User Defined Aircraft from the Toolbar at top of the screen.

Figure 8-11. Select "Create New User Defined Aircraft"

Figure 8-12 shows the UDA Vehicle Edit screen. Enter all the following data in the appropriate fields:

  1. New User Defined Aircraft. Enter a name for the UDA.
  2. Gross Taxi Weight. Enter the gross weight of the aircraft.
  3. Percent Gross Weight on Whole Main Gear. Enter the value as a decimal number between 0 and 1.0. In most cases, the value 0.95 is assumed for thickness design.
  4. PCR Percent Gross Weight on Gear. Enter the value of percent gross weight on the main gear to be used for ACR-PCR computations, as a decimal number between 0 and 1.0. This value, which is usually less than 0.95, may be obtained from the Aircraft Characteristics for Airport Planning manual published by the aircraft manufacturer. If the information is unknown or unavailable, enter 0.95 in this field.
  5. Tire Pressure. Enter the default tire pressure associated with the Gross Taxi Weight of the user defined aircraft.
  6. Gear Orientation. Enter the orientation of the main gear for the FAASR3D analysis as either 0 or 90. A value of 0 indicates the user expects the gear to cause the greatest stress at the midpoint of the longitudinal joint. A value of 90 indicates the user expects the gear to cause the greatest stress at the midpoint of the transverse joint.
  7. Tire Coordinates. Enter the horizontal coordinates of the tires in one main gear truck. The transverse (X) coordinate is defined with reference to the aircraft centerline. The tires will be reflected automatically on the other side of the aircraft longitudinal axis. The longitudinal (Y) coordinate origin is arbitrary but is typically at the center of the gear. It is not necessary to enter the dual tire spacing, tandem spacing or track spacing separately.

It is necessary to define at least one evaluation point, but there is no upper limit. This is necessary because the location of maximum strain can change from directly under the center of the tire for thin pavements to directly under the center of the gear for very thick pavements.
