title: Modes of Operation
html: FAARFIELD has four modes of operation: Design Mode, Life Mode, Life and Compaction Mode, and PCR Mode.

title: Design Mode
html:
Design Mode uses an iterative design procedure to determine the appropriate pavement thickness for a given traffic mix. It is selected by choosing Thickness Design for the analysis type. The user enters the traffic data and an estimated pavement structure. FAARFIELD will calculate the optimum thickness based on the design options. The steps for performing a pavement design are:

  1. Enter the pavement type.
  2. Adjust the layer types and parameters to approximate the expected design.
  3. Enter the design traffic mix.
  4. Select the Thickness Design analysis type.
  5. Click the Run button.
  6. View the design results by selecting the Section Report or CDF Graph on the Explorer tab.

Steps 1 through 4 may be performed in any order so long as all four steps are completed prior to step 5.

title: Pavement Life Mode
html:
Pavement Life Mode estimates the structural pavement life of a section by calculating how many years a given pavement structure can support a given traffic mix. FAARFIELD uses CDF concepts to determine how long the pavement will support the traffic. The steps for performing a pavement life analysis are:

  1. Enter the pavement type.
  2. Adjust the layer types and parameters to reflect the pavement structure.
  3. Enter the traffic mix.
  4. Select the Life analysis type.
  5. Click the Run button.
  6. The calculated pavement life is displayed in the Multi-Use area. Additional details are available in the Section Report and CDF Graph on the Explorer tab.

Steps 1 through 4 may be performed in any order so long as all four steps are completed prior to step 5.

title: Life and Compaction Mode
html:
In Life and Compaction Mode, FAARFIELD computes the subgrade compaction requirements for new flexible and new rigid pavement design based on the design traffic mix. The user should refer to AC 150/5320-6 to ensure that all applicable requirements for subgrade compaction and density control are met. To compute compaction requirements for a completed thickness design:

  1. Enter the pavement type.
  2. Adjust the layer types and parameters to reflect the pavement structure.
  3. Enter the traffic mix.
  4. Select the Compaction/Life analysis type.
  5. Click the Run button.
  6. The analysis results are available in the Section Report and CDF Graph on the Explorer tab.

Steps 1 through 4 may be performed in any order so long as all four steps are completed prior to step 5.

Minimum compaction requirements in FAARFIELD are based on the Compaction Index (CI) concept. CI is defined as the CBR required at a given depth to support a given gear load and number of repetitions. Hence, CI is essentially a CBR method in reverse. Curves have been developed relating the CI to required percent compaction of soils for both cohesive and non-cohesive soils. These curves were based on observations from full-scale and field tests on airports. However, to implement these curves in FAARFIELD, it was necessary to relate the CI to the vertical stress at different depths below the surface computed by FAARFIELD. The method is described in detail in the following reference:

Brill, D.R., and Chen, Y.G., "Automated Design-Based Compaction Criteria for Airport Pavements Using FAARFIELD," Proceedings of Ninth International Conference on the Bearing Capacity of Roads, Railways and Airfields, Trondheim, Norway, 2013, pp. 797-806.

After the execution of the Compaction/Life, results will be displayed in two tables in the Section Report. The first table refers to non-cohesive soils and the second to cohesive soils. Non-cohesive soils, for the purpose of determining compaction control, are those with a plasticity index (PI) less than 3. It is the responsibility of the design engineer to determine which of the two criteria is applicable for the site soils. Both tables contain a schedule of percentages of maximum dry density, and a range of depths for which the given minimum percentage applies. Depths in the second column reference the surface of the pavement, while the depths in the third column reference the top of the subgrade. The values in these columns should differ in the thickness of the pavement structure above the subgrade (with some error possibly due to rounding). Values in these columns should be used to establish compaction control points for placing and compacting the subgrade. The fourth column references the aircraft in the section design traffic mix that FAARFIELD used to compute the compaction requirement. Note: For mixed traffic, the critical airplane may be different for different depths and levels of compaction.

Percentages listed are percentages of maximum dry density, based on either the standard Proctor test (ASTM D698) for gross aircraft weights under 60,000 lbs., or the modified Proctor test (ASTM D 1557) for gross weights of 60,000 lbs. and above. FAARFIELD checks the design list and provides the applicable ASTM reference in the Subgrade Compaction Notes below the second table in the Section Report.

title: PCR Mode
html:
In PCR Mode, FAARFIELD computes the Pavement Classification Rating (PCR) for a pavement structure. The steps for performing a PCR analysis are:

  1. Enter the pavement type.
  2. Adjust the layer types and parameters to reflect the pavement structure.
  3. Enter the traffic mix.
  4. Select the PCR analysis type.
  5. Click the Run button.
  6. The PCR is displayed on the Status tab in the Multi-Use area. Additional details are available in the PCR Report and PCR Graph on the Explorer tab.

Steps 1 through 4 may be performed in any order so long as all three steps are completed prior to step 5.

The PCR is and indicator of the load carrying capacity of a pavement. The PCR is compared to the Aircraft Classification Rating (ACR) of aircraft in the traffic mix. An ACR smaller than the PCR indicates the pavement should be sufficient to support the traffic. An ACR larger than the PCR indicates the pavement may be structurally deficient. If Compute ACR for All Subgrade Categories is selected in Design Options, it will also calculate the ACR for the four subgrade categories defined in the ACR-PCR method. ACR/PCR is an improvement of the existing Aircraft Classification Number - Pavement Classification Number (ACN-PCN) method.

In 1977, a Study Group in ICAO developed a single international method of reporting pavement strengths, the ACN-PCN method (AC 150/5335-5C). This method expresses the effect of an individual aircraft on different pavements with a single unique number that varies according to aircraft weight and configuration, pavement type, and subgrade strength. The number is the Aircraft Classification Number (ACN). Conversely, the load-carrying capacity of a pavement can be expressed by a single unique number, without specifying a particular aircraft or detailed information about the pavement structure. The number is the Pavement Classification Number (PCN). The ACN-PCN system is implemented so a pavement with a particular PCN value can support an aircraft that has an ACN value equal to or less than the pavement's PCN value.

ACN is defined as a number that expresses the relative effect of an aircraft at a given configuration on a pavement structure for a specified standard subgrade strength. The first step to calculating the ACN is to determine the Equivalent Single Wheel Load (ESWL), which is a mathematical scheme converting a multiple-wheel gear to a single-wheel gear that has similar characteristics. It is a single tire that represents an equivalent damaging effect to the pavement as the multiple-wheel gear. The next step during the ACN calculation the ESWL is converted as the Derived Single Wheel Load (DSWL), indicating the ESWL has a tire inflated to 181 psi (1.25 MPa). The ACN is defined as two times the DSWL (expressed in thousands of kilograms). Additionally, the derived single wheel load is a function of the subgrade strength. The ACN is defined for the following four subgrade categories:

  1. High strength: CBR 15 (rigid pavement), above CBR 13 (flexible pavement)
  2. Medium strength: CBR 10 (rigid pavement), CBR 8 to 13 (flexible pavement)
  3. Low strength: CBR 6 (rigid pavement), CBR 4 to 8 (flexible pavement)
  4. Ultra-low strength: CBR 3 rigid pavement), CBR below 4 (flexible pavement)

To calculate ACN values, FAA developed the COMFAA program for calculating ACN values in accordance with the ACN-PCN method while the COMFAA program was translated from the ICAO Aerodrome Design Manual (https://comfaa.software.informer.com/3.0/). Specific ACN values for a particular aircraft can be obtained from the aircraft manufacturers.

PCN is defined as a number that expresses the load-carrying capacity of a pavement for unrestricted operations. The PCN rating established for a pavement indicates that the pavement is capable of supporting aircraft having an ACN of equal or lower magnitude. The ACN for comparison to the PCN must be the aircraft's ACN established for the particular pavement type and subgrade category as well as for the particular aircraft mass and characteristics. The PCN is expressed as a five-part code, separated by forward-slashes and initiated with a PCN numerical value, indicating the load-carrying capacity of the pavement.

Pavement Type:

  1. (F) Flexible Pavement
  2. (R) Rigid Pavement

Subgrade Strength:

  1. (A) High Strength
  2. (B) Medium Strength
  3. (C) Low Strength
  4. (D) Ultra Low Strength

Evaluation Method:

  1. (T) – Technical
  2. (U) - Aircraft experience

Tire Pressure:

  1. (W) Unlimited - No pressure limit
  2. (X) High - Pressure limited to 254 psi (1.75 MPa)
  3. (Y) Medium - Pressure limited to 181 psi (1.25 MPa)
  4. 4. (Z) Low -Pressure limited to 73 psi (0.50 MPa)

For example, a PCN of 78/F/B/W/T means that:

  1. the value indicating pavement's load-carrying capacity is 78
  2. the pavement is flexible (F)
  3. the pavement is on a medium-strength subgrade (B)
  4. the pavement has no limit on tire pressure (W)
  5. the value of 78 is calculated through technical evaluation (T)

However, there is an inconsistency between the ACN/PCN system and the recent pavement design methods. The current ACN-PCN system is generally outdated as it fails to perform accurately. An urgent need emerges to align the ACN/PCN system with the LEA pavement design methods into the ACR-PCR. The renewed ACR-PCR method can overcome the limitations of the current system and allow a full consideration of the most updated evolutions in the field. It will also benefit the airlines and ultimately the whole air transportation community by optimizing operating weights and frequencies, as opposed to the current over-conservative CBR-based system.

The empirical method does not consider the actual mechanical response of the pavement; the mechanistic-empirical method is now adopted and considers the pavement mechanical (stress-strain) response to aircraft loads as well as the pavement performance. A more accurate correlation is required between the pavement design practice and the rating system. The CBR design procedure is replaced by the Linear Elastic Analysis (LEA) for pavement design. The effect of modern and complex landing gear configurations and improved mechanical characteristics has been evolved, which is from equivalencies of single wheels, standard material for all wheels, and realistic pavement material considered explicitly for the pavement response computation.

ACR/PCR improves upon the ACN/PCN system by replacing the CBR design procedure by the LEA. The modulus of subgrade reaction for rigid pavements (k-value), and the CBR on top of the subgrade for flexible pavements are replaced by a unique soil characterization method (Modulus of elasticity, E), and always fall into four categories (High, medium, low and ultra-low).

By using the "CDF" concept, the LEA allows the knowledge of the contribution of each aircraft composing a traffic mix to the maximum damage produced by the total traffic. It will ease the pavement overload criteria taking full advantage of how the overload aircraft behaves when it is mixed in an existing traffic mix. The new ACR still relates to a DSWL but its calculation is done through the LEA for both flexible and rigid pavements.

The new PCR procedure is to determine one or several critical aircraft within a traffic mix and to make the aircraft equivalent to the traffic mix with an equivalent annual departure with CDF equal to 1.0, where critical aircraft weight(s) can be adjusted to Maximum Allowable Gross Weight (MAGW) to compute the aircraft's ACR(s) at MAGW. Therefore, the calculated ACR(s) should be the PCR(s), and the calculated PCR used is the maximum PCR.

The standard subgrade strength categories are changed for both flexible and rigid pavements as:

  1. Category A: 35,000 psi (241.3 MPa)
  2. Category B: 20,000 psi (137.9 MPa)
  3. Category C: 10,000 psi (69.0 MPa)
  4. Category D: 2,000 psi (13.8MPa)

title: Design Options
html:
Options and parameters for controlling how FAARFIELD performs designs and analyses are accessed from the Design Options item in Explorer Interface. This will open the Design Options interface, as illustrated in Figure 11-1. Options are divided into General Settings, which are visible in the interface by default, and Advanced Settings, which are normally used only by advanced users and are hidden by default.

Figure 11-1. Design Options Interface Location

title: General Settings
html: General settings are the design options that are commonly used. They include whether to perform certain calculations, generate certain output files, and what units the program should display.

title: Calculate HMA CDF
html: The Calculate HMA CDF Design Option enables the computation of CDF for an asphalt layer as part of a pavement design. The default setting is No. A final check of any design should include performing the pavement design with Calculate HMA CDF set to Yes.

title: Automatic Flexible Base Design
html: The Automatic Flexible Base Design Design Option enables an automatic design calculation for base layer thickness in new flexible pavements. The default value is Yes. FAARFIELD first designs the base layer thickness to comply with minimum base layer thickness requirements of AC 150/5320-6. FAARFIELD then designs the subbase layer thickness based on the new base layer thickness. This option applies only to new flexible pavements and the automatic flexible base design is not performed where one or more of the layers in a pavement structure is a user-defined layer. Setting the option to No causes FAARFIELD to compute the thickness of the subbase layer without affecting base layer thickness set by the user.

title: Output File
html: The Output File Design Option causes FAARFIELD to store detailed calculation results in files in the working directory C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\. The files are LeafSG.out, LeafAC.out, and FAASR3DPCC.out. The default setting is No.

title: Units
html: The Units Design Option causes FAARFIELD to display values in either Metric (SI) or US Customary units. The default setting is US Customary.

title: Allow Flexible Computation for Thick Overlays on PCC
html: The Allow Flexible Computation for Thick Overlays on PCC Design Option causes FAARFIELD to perform an alternate thickness design for HMA-on-rigid overlays, in which the section is treated as a flexible pavement structure, and the existing PCC surface layer (the layer to be overlaid) functions as a stiff base layer. In certain cases where a relatively thin existing PCC layer receives a thick HMA overlay, this alternate procedure results in a thinner overlay thickness requirement than the conventional HMA-on-rigid overlay procedure. FAARFIELD compares the results from both procedures and reports the thinner of the two in the final design. The default value is Yes.

title: Compute ACR for All Subgrade Categories
html:
The Compute ACR for All Subgrade Categories Design Option causes FAARFIELD to calculate and display the ACR value of each vehicle in the traffic mix for each subgrade category defined in the PCR method in the traffic interface, as shown in Figure 11-2. Scroll to the right to see these values. The default value is No. Setting the option to Yes will increase running time.

Figure 11-2. ACR and PCR Values in the Traffic Interface

title: Show/Hide Advanced Options
html: The Show/Hide Advanced Options design option displays or hides the Advanced Options for FAARFIELD.

title: Set as Program Default
html: The Set as Program Default button stores the current design options as the default settings FAARFIELD will use with the next time the software is opened. The stored default settings can be returned to the initial settings provided by FAA using the Reset Default to Initial button.

title: Reset Default to Initial
html: The Reset Default to Initial button resets the default design options to their original settings provided by FAA. It removes all default settings configured by the user.

title: Show/Hide Pavement Image
html: The Show/Hide Pavement Image is used to show or hide the pavement image on the Structure tab in the Multi-Use area. Click the button to hide the image. When hidden, the structure tab is blank and editing a structure with the image is disabled. Click the button again to show the image.

title: Change Pavement Graphics
html:
FAARFIELD provides two sets of patterns for the pavement structure image: a hatch-based pattern shown in Figure 11-3 and photo-realistic images shown in Figure 11-4. The Change Pavement Graphics button switches between the two patterns. The default setting is the hatch-based pattern.

Figure 11-3. Hatch-Based Pavement Graphic

Figure 11-4. Photo-Realistic Pavement Graphic Pattern

title: User Defined Aircraft Directory
html: FAARFIELD allows the user to select the directory used for UDA's. The default directory is C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\User Defined Aircraft. When a user selects a different directory, FAARFIELD unloads the UDA's currently listed in the aircraft library and loads the UDA's in selected directory. UDA's are not removed from sections or jobs when a user selects a new UDA directory. FAARFIELD will remember the user's UDA directory between sessions.

title: Advanced Options
html:
Clicking the Show Advanced Options shows additional options for the user to customize the pavement design procedure, as shown in Figure 11-5. These advanced options are for special needs or advanced users. The default values for advanced options are suitable for the average requirements of most FAARFIELD users.

Figure 11-5. Design Options with Show Advanced Options

title: CDF Tolerance
html: The design of new flexible pavements, HMA on flexible overlays, new rigid pavements, and PCC on flexible overlays is a goal-seeking iterative process with a goal of CDFls 1. The CDF tolerance design option defines the convergence tolerance on the computed CDF, i.e., the goal is met when CDF = 1.0 +/- tolerance. The user can input CDF tolerance values in a range from 0.005 to 0.05. The larger the specified tolerance the faster the convergence but, the solution will be less accurate. The default value is set to 0.005 for maximum accuracy.

title: Life Tolerance (years)
html: Design of HMA on rigid overlays, unbonded PCC on rigid overlays, and partially bonded PCC on rigid overlays is a goal-seeking iterative process with a goal of the computed life equaling the design life. The Life Tolerance design option defines the convergence tolerance on the computed life in years. The user can input values for Life Tolerance in a range from 0.02 to 0.5 years. The larger the specified tolerance, the faster the convergence, but the solution will be less accurate. The default value is set at 0.4 years.

title: Alternate Subgrade
html: The Alternate Subgrade design option allows one of the upper layers in a pavement structure to be set as the effective subgrade layer for design. It is used in conjunction with relocation of the design layer. For example, this option allows the inclusion of stiff bottom layers in the structure. This option causes FAARFIELD to base the design on the vertical strain at the top of the layer below the design layer. This option only applies to flexible pavement designs. The default setting for this option is No.

title: N Section Parameter
html: The N Section Parameter design option applies only to unbonded PCC on rigid and partially bonded PCC on rigid overlay structures. It defines the number of traffic intervals for which the elastic modulus of the PCC base layer is recalculated. The default value is 16. Lower values of N section parameter will lead to faster convergence, and also less accuracy. Additional information on this topic can be found at: Rollings, R.S., FAA Technical Report DOT/FAA/PM-87/19, "Design of Overlays for Rigid Airport Pavements," April 1988, pages 103-107.

title: Partially Bonded Overlay on Rigid
html:
The Partially Bonded Overlay on Rigid is defined as a PCC-on-rigid overlay where no particular attempt is made to either eliminate or achieve bond between the concrete overlay and the existing rigid pavement. For the same design inputs, the thickness of a partially bonded PCC overlay falls between bonded and fully unbonded overlays. Partially bonded PCC on rigid overlays are no longer considered standard FAA designs in AC 150/5320-6. Therefore, by default, the Partially Bonded Overlay on Rigid design option is No.

If set to Yes, a message will be displayed: "Non-Standard Structure". The P-501 PCC Overlay (partially bonded) item will be shown in the material library, as illustrated in Figure 11-6. It is available only in the material library and is not available when editing the pavement structure using the image. It must be added to the structure as the top layer via drag-and-drop from the material library to the pavement structure grid.

Figure 11-6. P-501 PCC Overlay (Partially Bonded) Material

title: Section Notes
html: The Section Notes are part of the Notes and Design Options interface. They allow the user to record general information about a pavement section.

title: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html:
Thickness designs can be performed for seven general types of pavement structures:

  1. New Flexible (stabilized base)
  2. New flexible (aggregate base)
  3. HMA on Flexible
  4. HMA on Rigid
  5. New Rigid
  6. PCC on Flexible
  7. Unbonded on Rigid

New Flexible, HMA on Flexible, and New Rigid pavements are designed with the following general procedure:

  1. Create a pavement structure, a traffic mix, and set the Design Life.
  2. Click Run. This causes the thickness of a prescribed layer to be automatically adjusted by the program until the design criteria are satisfied.
  3. Inspect the structure when the design program has stopped running and, if necessary, manually adjust the thickness of other layers in the structure and click Run again. Repeat until the thickness design is satisfactory.
  4. Click Save Job. This saves all the information for the new structure to disk in a job file and marks the section as a completed design.

The automatic adjustment of the prescribed layer in step 2 is done by FAARFIELD as follows:

  1. Calculate the maximum stress or strain just above or below a layer interface for each vehicle in the traffic mix.
  2. Calculate the allowable number of airplane departures to failure for each airplane based on a defined relationship between allowable departures and either stress or strain.
  3. Find the ratio of actual departures to allowable departures for each airplane, this is the CDFeach airplane.
  4. Add the airplane CDFs together to find the overall CDF for the structure.
  5. Adjust the thickness of the prescribed layer until structure CDF = 1. (Increasing thickness decreases CDF.)

Design for overlays on rigid pavements is generally similar in terms of structure definition, traffic mix selection, and program execution, but the design procedures require more steps because deterioration of the existing pavement is considered. More details are provided below for the design of each of the different types of pavement structures.

title: New Flexible and HMA on Flexible
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html:
Subgrade vertical strain and horizontal strain at the bottom of all asphalt layers are the design criteria for New Flexible, HMA on Aggregate, and HMA on Flexible. With the fixed asphalt modulus values defined in the program, horizontal strain only becomes the dominant criterion when the structure is very deep and is heavily loaded. Under these conditions the horizontal strain also has a tendency to increase as the pavement depth increases, which is the opposite trend for subgrade strain. Overlap of the CDF can therefore occur, and a proper design is never realized. For these reasons, and to save run time, the subgrade strain is used to iterate to a subgrade CDF equal to 1.0. Only one evaluation depth needs to be sent to LEAF and the run time is approximately halved for deep, multiple layered structures (compared to computing subgrade and asphalt strain each time).

When the subgrade criterion has been satisfied, a final calculation is made to find the asphalt CDF (again using only one evaluation depth). If the structure is saved after design without making any modifications, the section data is marked as a completed design and the asphalt CDF stored in the job file section data record. The value of the asphalt CDF can be viewed in the Section Report. By default, the program does not compute asphalt CDF. To check asphalt CDF after achieving a design that satisfies the subgrade criterion, the user should switch on the Calculate HMA CDF in the Design Options. If the Calculate HMA CDF is Yes, the design continues to run after the displayed (subgrade) CDF has reached its terminal value. A message will display stating that the asphalt CDF is computing. The value of the asphalt CDF is displayed once the computation is complete.

For new flexible designs, the thickness of the layer immediately above the subgrade (the design layer, indicated by the small arrow to the left of the structure) is adjusted to make the subgrade CDF approximately equal to one. The design will terminate when CDF is in the range 0.995 to 1.005 based on FAARFIELD's default error control. This tolerance can be temporarily changed from the Design Options. If during the design procedure, the design layer becomes thinner than its allowable minimum thickness, then the thickness of the layer above is halved, or set to its minimum thickness, and the procedure continues. If the CDF is still less than one with both of the adjusted layers at their minimum thicknesses, the final value of CDF is displayed and the design terminated along with a message that minimum thicknesses have been reached. This procedure is not intended to "optimize" a design, it is intended only to protect from inappropriate input data.

Minimum aggregate base course thickness requirements are given in AC 150/5320-6. In FAARFIELD, new flexible pavements with a standard crushed aggregate base layer (P-209 or P-208) and standard subbase layer (P-154), the base course thickness is computed as the thickness required to protect the subbase (which is assumed to have a CBR value of 20). However, a minimum aggregate base course thickness (6 inches) is enforced for constructability. The minimum thickness of stabilized base courses per AC 150/5320-6 is 5 inches. However, this assumes that the subbase material is improved to P-209 or equal quality. If a stabilized base layer is placed on standard (P-154) subbase, then FAARFIELD will design the base layer to the thickness needed to protect the subbase, assuming that the subbase provides CBR 20 at the top.

For overlay design, the top layer is always the design layer. The thickness of the top layer is automatically adjusted to make the subgrade strain CDF equal to one. The procedure is terminated and displays a message if the top layer reaches its minimum allowable thickness.

A.1 HMA Overlay on Rigid Pavement

The design of HMA overlay on rigid pavement is similar to that of PCC Overlay on Rigid Pavement. In both cases, the deterioration of the SCI of the existing PCC is considered. The design terminates when the terminal SCI is reached, and the difference between the calculated and desired design life is less than a given tolerance, which by default is 0.4 years. The value of the terminal SCI in the life computation is either 40 or 57, depending on the base/subbase structure. FAARFIELD does not consider the contribution of reflection crack propagation through the HMA overlay thickness to the computed life of the overlay.

The FAARFIELD HMA on Rigid design procedure is most appropriate when designing relatively thin HMA overlays on PCC in good-to-excellent condition, that is, when the overlaid pavement can be expected to behave structurally as a rigid pavement. In the case of thick HMA overlays on relatively thin or deteriorated PCC pavements, it may be more economical to treat the design problem as essentially a flexible pavement design, with the overlay as the design layer and the existing PCC acting as a stiff base layer. Selecting the Allow Flexible Computation for Thick Overlays on PCC design option enables FAARFIELD to do both types of computations and selecting the design procedure that results in a more economical (thinner) HMA overlay. Note: The flexible pavement option will not result in an HMA overlay thinner than the existing PCC slab.

title: New Rigid Pavement
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html:
For New Rigid Pavement design, CDFalculated using the larger of (a) the horizontal edge stress at the bottom of the PCC layer, or (b) the horizontal interior slab stress. To account for load transfer of adjacent slabs, the free edge stress is computed for the gear load and reduced by 25%. For gear loading along the slab edge, it is necessary to select an orientation. The general procedure is to compute 75 percent of the free edge stress with the gear oriented parallel to the slab edge, and 75 percent of the edge stress with the gear oriented perpendicular to the slab edge, and then select the higher of the two cases as the working edge stress for design. However, for the majority of gear configurations it is based on priority which orientation will yield the critical stress, so it is not necessary for FAARFIELD to do more than one computation per gear. Edge stresses for rigid pavements are computed using the three-dimensional finite element model. The slab dimensions are fixed by the program and cannot be changed by the user. Interior stresses are computed using LEAF based on a linear elastic model. The interior stress is assumed to be 95% of the maximum horizontal stress computed by LEAF.

Parameters were obtained by analyzing failures of full-scale rigid pavement test pavements at the National Airport Pavement Test Facility (NAPTF), as well as previous full-scale tests. In such failure data there is inherently a considerable amount of scatter. This transition reflects the fact that thinner PCC pavements on strong foundations are more likely to experience top-down cracking (e.g., corner breaks) than pavements on weaker foundations. Since the top-down cracking failure mode is not considered in FAARFIELD design, the use of the more conservative 85% failure curve is justified for higher subgrade strengths. Note that parameters b and d have constant values in the FAARFIELD failure model and are not a function of E.

Failure for a rigid pavement in FAARFIELD is defined as SCI= 80. For a new rigid pavement, the program iterates on the thickness of the PCC layer (the design layer) until the failure model predicts a value of SCI=80 at the end of the design life (20 years for standard designs). The number of coverages to failure (C) is therefore the number of coverages for SCI = 80 at any given value of R/σ (Parker, F., Jr., W.R. Barker, R.C. Gunkel, and E.C. Odom, Development of a Structural Design Procedure for Rigid Airport Pavements, Report No. FAA RD 77 81, April 1977).

The failure model above assumes that the SCI deteriorates under traffic as a linear function of the logarithm of coverages (after first reaching the first structural crack). The factor is used to adjust the slope of the line when the structure includes a higher quality (stabilized) base. When the concrete slab is placed on an 8-inch thick crushed aggregate (P-209) layer, or on a 4-inch thick stabilized layer (500,000 psi), the value of is one and the basic (uncompensated) failure model is recovered. But if the thickness or quality of the base/subbase structure is greater than either of these two conditions, decreases, and the number of coverages to failure increases. Adjusting the slope of the line in this way recognizes that a PCC slab placed on a stabilized base will not deteriorate as rapidly following the appearance of a first crack compared to a similar slab on a conventional (aggregate) base.

title: PCC Overlay on Flexible Pavement
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html: When the PCC Overlay on Flexible Pavement layer is placed over an asphalt surface or undefined layer, the new rigid pavement design procedure is automatically executed.

title: PCC Overlay on Rigid Pavement
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html: PCC Overlay designs procedures are divided into Unbonded and Partially Bonded methods. Bonded overlays are treated as New Rigid designs.

title: Unbonded PCC Overlay on Rigid Pavement
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html: Placing a PCC overlay on top of a PCC surface layer causes FAARFIELD to execute the concrete overlay on rigid pavement design procedure. Standard PCC overlays are fully unbonded. An option to design partially bonded overlays is available in FAARFIELD, but it is disabled by default. Within the three-dimensional finite element model, an appropriate value of horizontal interface stiffness is assigned internally based on the overlay type selected. A third type of overlay, bonded concrete overlay, should be treated as a new rigid pavement with the thickness of the PCC layer equal to the sum of the overlay and existing PCC thicknesses, according to the applicable provisions of AC 150/5320-6. For both unbonded and partially bonded overlays, the maximum tensile stress at the bottom of the overlay is used as the critical response in the calculation ofCDF many unbonded overlay designs, a thin asphalt leveling course is used to break the bond between the existing PCC and the new overlay. In FAARFIELD, the leveling course provides no structural contribution, so it does not appear as a separate structural layer. The engineer should remember that the total thickness displayed on the FAARFIELD screen does not include the additional thickness of any asphalt bond breaker course.

title: Partially Bonded PCC Overlay on Rigid Pavement
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html:
Partially bonded PCC overlays are not considered standard designs in AC 150/5320-6. Therefore, by default, design of a partially bonded PCC on rigid overlays is disabled. The option may be enabled from Design Options, however, if a partially bonded PCC on rigid overlay is selected, the following message will be displayed: "Non-Standard Structure."

The design starts with a trial overlay thickness selected by the user. CDF is calculated for the concrete overlay layer using the same model that is used in new rigid pavement designs. However, the elastic modulus of the existing PCC is assumed to decrease as a function of decreasing SCI. Thus, the tensile stress in the overlay layer varies during the life of the overlay, and the CDF of the structure must be computed by numerical integration. This results in solution times that are typically much longer than those for the other pavement types. After the CDF has been calculated, the thickness of the overlay is adjusted to bring the next calculated CDF closer to a value of 1 for the correct design life. The design is terminated when the calculated value of CDF range is between 0.995 and 1.005 and the difference between the calculated and desired design life is less than a given tolerance, which by default is 0.4 years.

title: Overlays on Composite Pavements
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html: Design of overlays on existing rigid pavements which already have an asphalt overlay cannot be done directly using FAARFIELD because a PCC surface layer cannot be placed further down than the second layer in a structure. One method of representing such a structure is to replace the PCC layer in the existing pavement with a user-defined layer or a variable stabilized layer. The modulus of the substitute layer can be selected based on the design engineer's judgment of the SCI of the existing PCC layer and application of the equation for PCC layer modulus given in the PCC overlay design example.

title: Solutio n Times
group: APPENDIX A: Theoretical Approach to Pavement Design Procedures
html:
For flexible pavements, the execution time required to design a structure is almost completely dependent on the floating point performance of the computer when performing the layered elastic strain and stress calculations. Execution time is roughly proportional to the total number of "design" wheels for all of the airplanes in the design list, and is proportional to a smaller power of the number of layers in the structure. This is because the inner loop in LEAF consumes almost all of the solution time.

In general, rigid pavement designs take much longer to execute than flexible pavement designs. This is because the 3-dimensional finite element models used in the rigid pavement procedures are computationally intense. The run time for finite element based designs depends on many factors, including the processor speed and available RAM, the number of airplanes in the design mix, and the number of structural layers. However, the number of wheels in the loading gear is not a significant factor. But rigid overlay designs take significantly longer to execute than new rigid designs.

FAARFIELD implements a number of computational strategies designed to minimize computation time. Among these is the use of a preliminary design running LEAF prior to performing the final design iterations based on the three-dimensional finite element model. This eliminates time-consuming and unnecessary finite element computations and also allows airplanes making a negligible contribution (<0.005) to the CDF to be removed from the analysis during finite element processing. (These airplanes will still appear in the airplane list in all program outputs, but their CDF contribution is reported as zero.)

Thick aggregate layers increase the solution time more than would be expected because of the sublayering used to represent variations of modulus with depth. Thin concrete overlays on rigid pavements have the longest solution times of all the structure types.

title: APPENDIX B: Cumulative Damage Factor
html:
Cumulative damage factor (CDF) is the amount of the structural fatigue life of a pavement that has been used up. It is expressed as the ratio of applied load repetitions to allowable load repetitions to failure, or, for one airplane and constant annual departures:

When CDF = 1,

the pavement will have used up all of its fatigue life.

When CDF < 1,

the pavement will have some life remaining, and the value of CDF will give the fraction of the life used.

When CDF > 1,

all of the fatigue life will have been used up and the pavement will have failed.

Note: In these definitions, failure means failure in a particular structural failure mode according to the assumptions and definitions on which the design procedures are based. A value of CDF greater than one does not necessarily mean that the pavement will no longer support traffic, but that it will have failed according to the definition of failure used in the design procedure, and within the constraints of uncertainties in material property assumptions, etc. Nevertheless, the thickness design is based on the assumption that failure occurs when CDF = 1.

Multiple airplane types are accounted for by using Miner's Rule:

CDF = CDF1 + CDF2 + ... CDFN

Where CDFI is the CDF for each airplane type in the mix and N is the number of airplane types in the mix.

Note: If the same airplane model operates on a pavement at two or more significantly different weights, each operating weight is treated as a distinct airplane type for the purpose of Miner's rule.

FAARFIELD computes a separate CDF for each failure mode included in the design procedure. For example, in flexible pavement design, the thickness is adjusted to make the CDF for subgrade failure equal to 1. An additional computation is then made to find the CDF for asphalt fatigue cracking. If the asphalt CDF is found to be less than 1, the asphalt is predicted not to fail in cracking before the subgrade fails. But if the asphalt CDF is greater than 1, the asphalt is predicted to fail before the subgrade, and adjustments should be made to base and subbase layers so that asphalt CDF is less than 1 in the final design.

In the FAARFIELD program implementation, CDF is calculated for each 10-inch wide strip along the pavement over a total width of 820 inches. Pass-to-coverage ratio is computed for each strip based on a normally distributed airplane wander pattern with standard deviation of 30.5 inches (equivalent to airplane operation on a taxiway) and used in the above equation for Miner's rule. The CDF for design is taken to be the maximum over all 82 strips. Even with the same gear geometry, therefore, airplanes with different main gear track widths will have different pass-to-coverage ratios in each of the 10-inch strips and may show little cumulative effect on the maximum CDF. For this reason, removing the airplane with the lowest stress or strain may have little effect on the design thickness, depending on how close the gear tracks are to each other.

title: APPENDIX D: Data Files
html: This appendix addresses output files and storage files used by FAARFIELD, along with file management.

title: File Management
html: In general, file management, such as backup and deletion, should be done with Windows Explorer. The Toolbar provides functions for saving job files. The job file can be saved anywhere within the computer's system.

title: Output Data Files
html:
At the end of the structural design or life computation, details of the structure, airplane loads, and pavement responses are stored in an ASCII text output file and placed in the working directory. The output files always have the same names and overwrite the files generated by the previous computation. The filenames are:

  1. LeafSG.out (subgrade responses for a flexible pavement)
  2. LeafAC.out (asphalt surface layer responses for a flexible pavement)
  3. Compaction.out (subgrade responses for compaction requirement)

For flexible pavements, stresses, strains, and displacements are given for each evaluation point for each airplane in the traffic mix. Principal and octahedral stresses are included. LeafSG.out contains the responses computed at the top of the subgrade, and LeafAC.out contains the data for responses computed at the bottom of the asphalt surface layer.

Note: Output files will not be created if the Output File design option is No.

title: Storage Files
html:
FAARFIELD stores information concerning each job in a job file with the extension *.jobx. FAARFIELD can also read job files from version 1.42 of the software that have the extension *.job.xml. Job files can be stored anywhere on the user's system. Job files contain all pertinent information for computations, including user-defined vehicle information, and may be emailed or otherwise shared with other users. The default location for job file storage is:

C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\

The vehicle library is stored in a cryptographically signed XML file in user's working directory. It contains the information for each vehicle that is required for FAARFIELD to perform a design or analysis with that vehicle. FAARFIELD uses the cryptographic signature to determine if the aircraft library has been altered. If FAARFIELD detects the file has been altered, a warning is given at startup and all resulting designs are considered non-standard. The vehicle library file storage is located at:

C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\Defaults\Aircraft\aircraft.xml

FAA may periodically issue updates to the vehicle library by publishing a new cryptographically signed aircraft library file. To update FAARFIELD, replace the file above with the updated aircraft.xml file. Users do not require administrative privileges to update the vehicle library. Note that job files contain complete information for the traffic mixes used in that job. Job files created before the vehicle library was updated will contain vehicle data from the old vehicle library. This data will not automatically be updated the next time the job file is opened. Users must remove the old vehicles from the traffic mix and re-add vehicles from the updated vehicle library.

User Defined Vehicles are stored in XML format. The XML schema is identical to that used for the vehicle library. FAARFIELD stores data for each UDA in a separate file, although it is possible for a single UDA file to contain data for more than one vehicle. UDA files may be shared with other users. UDA files are stored in:

C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\User Defined Aircraft\

FAARFIELD scans this directory for UDA files with extension *.xml on startup. Vehicles from UDA files in this directory are listed in the External Library category of the vehicle library in the Explorer.

Stored traffic mixes are saved as XML files. Traffic mixes contain a complete record of the vehicles and vehicle properties, including UDA's. They may be shared with other users. Stored traffic mix files are in:

C:\...\Documents\My FAARFIELD\TrafficLibrary\

FAARFIELD scans this directory for stored traffic mix files with extension *.xml on startup. Traffic mixes in this directory are available in the Traffic Interface.

title: APPENDIX E: Design Examples
html: The design examples cover the major functions of the FAARFIELD, which include four pavement types and four running modes. The four pavement types are New Flexible, New Rigid, HMA on Rigid, and Unbonded on Rigid. The four running modes are Thickness Design, Life, Compaction/Life, and PCR. Examples are also given to illustrate overlay design on composite pavements and the effects of sublayering in aggregate layers. Percent annual growth is assumed to be zero in all of the examples. Also, layer thickness results are all given to 1 decimal place. Rounding would be done before writing the final design specifications.

title: New Flexible Design Example
html:
The pavement in the new flexible pavement design example is to service airplanes of greater than 100,000 lbs. gross weight, and must therefore have a stabilized base and subbase as specified in AC 150/5320-6. Item P-401, Plant Mix Bituminous Pavement, is selected for the base course and Item P-209, Crushed Aggregate Base Course, is selected for the subbase. The thickness of the HMA surface layer is 5 inches, which exceeds the minimum thickness of 4 inches required by AC 150/5320-6. The subgrade CBR for the example is 8. The design life is 20 years, complying with AC 150/5320-6. The determination and selection of suitable base and subbase thicknesses is discussed below after describing the initial setup of the example.

When FAARFIELD is started, a new job with a new section is already created by the program with default parameters and no pavement structure or traffic mix is selected as shown in Figure E-1.

Figure E-1. Starting FAARFIELD

Traffic mix is chosen to represent a heavily loaded pavement as would be found at a major airport as shown in Figure E-2.

Figure E-2. Traffic Mix for Heavily Loaded Airport Pavement

To start up the Thickness Design with a new job file:

  1. Change or retain the default names for both new job and new section.
  2. Note that the Thickness Design is the default Running Mode.
  3. Select a pavement type where the New Flexible is chosen for the design example.
  4. Click the Stored Aircraft Mix to select the saved traffic mix "Design Examples".
  5. Retain the Design Options the default setting.
  6. Modify the properties of the pavement structure and traffic mix if needed.
  7. Click Save Job to save the names for both new job and new section before the execution.

The changes in the example that needs to make are to change the thickness of the HMA surface layer from the default value of 4 to the actual value of 5 inches, and to change the subgrade CBR from 10 to 8 (Figure E-3). The modification can be done by either through the Pavement Grid or Structure image in the Multi-Use area.

The thickness of 5 inches for the P-401/P403 base layer will be used as a starting point. By default, FAARFIELD will automatically compute the required base or subbase layer thickness to comply with the structural requirements and minimum thickness required by AC 150/5320-6.

Figure E-3. FAARFIELD Settings before New Flexible Design Execution

Click the Run. The program will automatically compute base and subbase thicknesses. In this case, the computed stabilized base thickness is 5.0 inches and the subbase one is 18.8 inches. Subgrade CDF = 1.0, indicating that the subgrade (vertical strain) design criterion has been satisfied (Figure E-4).

Figure E-4. New Flexible Thickness Design Results

To perform the final design run, open the Design Options and switch on the Calculate HMA CDF. Again, click the Run. Then the program gives a subbase thickness of 18.5 inches, but this time it also reports that HMA CDF = 0.17. Since 0.17 < 1.0 (Figure E-5), the design is acceptable for the HMA fatigue (horizontal strain) design criterion.

Figure E-5. New Flexible Thickness Design Results with Computed HMA CDF

Next, compute the Life as verification of the thickness design results, which is supposed to be 20 years due to the 20-year-based thickness design process. Change the mode to Life and click the Run. Results show that the computed life equals 20 years with Subgrade and HMA CDFs unchanged. The verification is done (Figure E-6).

Figure E-6. New Flexible Life Results with Subgrade and HMA CDF

For this example, a base thickness of 5.0 inches was finally selected. After the final design run, the subbase thickness of 18.8 inches gives a total pavement thickness of 28.8 inches. By clicking the Section Report, the report for the final design is shown and can be save by clicking the Save As PDF on the top of the report (Figure E-7 to Figure E-14). HMA CDF is also reported for both HMA layers in the structure, the P-401/P-403 HMA surface layer as well as the P-401/P-403 HMA stabilized base. From Figure E-7 to Figure E-14, it is clear that the HMA base layer is the critical layer for asphalt fatigue, although the subgrade strain criterion controls the design as a whole.

Figure E-7. New Flexible Job Information

Figure E-8. New Flexible Pavement Structure Information by Layer

Figure E-9. New Flexible Airplane Information

Figure E-10. New Flexible Additional Airplane Information (Subgrade CDF)

Figure E-11. New Flexible Additional Airplane Information (HMA CDF)

Figure E-12. New Flexible Additional Airplane Information (P-401/P-403 HMA Stabilized CDF)

Figure E-13. Embedded Calculated Pavement Image in New Flexible Section Report

Figure E-14. Save As PDF for New Flexible Section Report

Note that the wing gear and the belly gear for the B747-400, A340-200 std, and A340-300 opt are all treated as separate airplanes in the design procedure. Also, the thickness of the subgrade is given as 0 inches. This reflects the assumption in the layered elastic representation of the structure is that the subgrade is infinitely thick.

Clicking the CDF Graph shows that the critical Cumulative CDF occurs on the top of the subgrade at offset of around 220 inches (Figure E-15). The aircraft to the critical CDF is B747-400 with subgrade CDF contribution of 0.4. To save the CDF graph report, click the Save As PDF on the top of the report.

Figure E-15. New Flexible CDF Graph

By running the Compaction/Life analysis, the subgrade compaction requirements are also given in the section report (Figure E-16). To save the report, click the Save As PDF on the top of the report. Although the B747-400 has the highest contribution to the Subgrade CDF (due to high levels of traffic) in this example, the A350-1000 governs the subgrade compaction requirement. Assuming that in this case the subgrade soils are cohesive, only the top 3 inches of subgrade would need to be compacted to 95%. However, due to the heavy traffic loads anticipated, the next 49 inches should be compacted to at least 90% of modified Proctor density. If the subgrade is in cut, and existing in-place densities are not sufficient to meet the 90% requirement, then additional compaction may be required.

Figure E-16. New Flexible Subgrade Compaction Requirements for NonCohesive and Cohesive Soil

To compute the ACR thickness and ACR, switch the mode to PCR and click the Run. Before execution, switch the Compute ACR for All Subgrade Categories design option to Yes. The PCR results are given in the PCR Report, PCR Graph, and Form 5010. The results are shown in Figure E-17 to Figure E-22 below with wing gear and belly gear separated. The subgrade is categorized as C(11k) according to the four subgrade categories: 2000 psi (D), 10,000 psi (C), 20,000 psi (B), and 35,000 psi (A). Figure E-18 shows the general traffic data input from the traffic mix with a 20 years coverage. Figure E-19 exhibits the critical ACR thick and PCR on C(11k), which is caused by A350-900. It also has the critical aircraft ACR calculated at its MGW. Figure E-20 shows the flexible ACR at indicated gross weight and strength of all aircraft. It lists all the ACR Thick for each aircraft as well as the ACR values at four subgrade categories. To save all the reports, click the Save As PDF on the top of the report.

The PCR Graph in Figure E-21 shows ACR/PCR against annual departures with wing gear and belly gear not separated. The highest annual departures in red line falls into the B747-400. However, the aircraft ACR in blue square bar gives the maximum value of 743.5 by A350-900. The calculated PCR in black line is determined according to the critical aircraft ACR, which is 770.6 here by A350-900. Therefore, the PCR 771/F/C/X/T in the Form 5010 (D-22) means that:

  1. the value indicating pavement's load-carrying capacity is 771
  2. the pavement is flexible (F)
  3. the pavement is on a low-strength subgrade (C)
  4. the pavement has a maximum tire pressure of 253.8 psi (1.75 MPa) (X)
  5. the value of 771 is calculated through technical evaluation (T)

title: New Rigid Design Example
html:
The new rigid design example uses the same traffic mix as the new flexible design example, and the pavement for the new rigid design example must therefore have a stabilized subbase course to satisfy the requirements of AC 150/5320-6. A 2-layer subbase has been selected with Item P-304, Cement Treated Base (CTB), at the top and Item P-209, Crushed Aggregate Base Course below. The subgrade k value is 120 pci and the surface is Item P-501, Portland Cement Concrete Pavement, with a design flexural strength of 675 psi. Design life is 20 years.

The preparation steps are similar to the example in the New Flexible Design Example. The traffic mix is the same (Figure E-2). The subgrade k value and the PCC flexural strength are both changed. P-501 concrete has a default flexural strength R = 650 psi but change it to R = 675 psi. The subgrade k value is changed from 172.4 to 120.0 pci. The thickness of P-304 CTB is changed from 6 to 8 inches in this example. The modification can be done by either through the Pavement Grid or Structure image from the Section Interface.

Click Run. The program will automatically compute base and subbase thicknesses. The thickness of the top layer is iterated until the CDF for tensile stress at the bottom of the surface layer has a value of 1.0. In this case the computed PCC surface thickness is 17.0 inches for a PCC CDF of 1.0 (Figure E-23).

By running Compaction/Life, the percent CDFU is 174.56 with PCC CDF of 1.0, and calculated life is verified as 20 years in the Status (Figure E-24). The subgrade compaction requirements are computed and results are given in the section report (Figure E-25 to Figure E-29). To save the section report, click the Save As PDF on the top of the report.

Clicking CDF Graph shows that the critical Cumulative CDF occurs on the top of the subgrade at offset of around 220 inches (Figure E-30). The aircraft to the critical CDF is A350-1000 with subgrade CDF contribution of 0.4. To save the CDF graph report, click the Save As PDF on the top of the report.

Figure E-23. New Rigid Thickness Design Results

Figure E-24. New Rigid Compaction/Life Results with %CDFU, PCC CDF, and Life

Note that the Poisson's ratio for PCC and subgrade here are 0.15 and 0.4, respectively. Additional Airplane Information shows that in this case the PCC CDF on the critical entry is mostly contributed by only three airplanes, the A350-900, A350-1000, and B747-400; the other airplanes in the traffic mix do not contribute significantly to the total damage. A350-1000 takes the critical PCC CDF to this example, which is followed by A350-900.

In the subgrade compaction requirements, A350-900 is by computation the critical airplane for the compaction, while only A350-1000 is highlighted by the requirements. Assuming that in this case the subgrade soils are cohesive, the top 41 inches of subgrade would need to be compacted to 85%; for non-cohesive, the top 9 inches of subgrade would need to be compacted to 95%.

So, the A350-1000 is the critical airplane in the traffic mix for computing compaction requirements. Note that for rigid pavements, depending on whether the subgrade is in cut or fill, the FAARFIELD-computed requirement may or may not be more restrictive than the minimum compaction requirements for rigid pavements in AC 150/5320-6. It is the responsibility of the design engineer to check the AC to see that all applicable standards are satisfied.

title: PCC Overlay on Rigid Design Example
html:
Design of an overlay on a rigid pavement normally starts with an existing pavement structure having a known SCI. In this design example, an unbonded overlay is to be applied over an existing rigid pavement which has an SCI of 70. The traffic mix is the same as in Figure E-2. For the PCC overlay, a concrete strength of 650 psi will be used. The design subgrade k-value is 120 pci. The properties of the existing structure are shown in Figure E-37.

Figure E-37. New Rigid Pavement Structure Information by Layer

After setting up the structure to match the information above and setting the traffic information, as described in the new pavement design examples, an overlay layer is to be added in the Section Interface. Add the P-501 PCC Overlay (unbonded) onto the P-501 PCC Surface through the Material in the Explorer Interface or the Pavement image in the Section Interface. Highlight the SCI box and change the value to 70 from default value of 80 (Figure E-38). Percent CDFU will default to a value of 100. It cannot be changed in this example because SCI is less than 100.

Run the Thickness Design. This process will take considerably longer than in the new pavement designs. For the PCC overlay, FAARFIELD computes a thickness of 5.0 inches. The total structure thickness is 36.0 inches. The final structure with airplane information is shown in Figure E-39 to Figure E-42. A350-900 takes the critical PCC CDF to this example.

Figure E-38. PCC Overlay on Rigid Thickness Design Setting

Figure E-39. PCC Overlay on Rigid Pavement Structure Information by Layer

Figure E-40. PCC Overlay on Rigid Airplane Information

Figure E-41. PCC Overlay on Rigid Additional Airplane Information

Figure E-42. PCC Overlay on Rigid CDF Graph

In the output from the section report, the modulus of the PCC surface layer of the existing structure is given as 4,000,000 psi. But this is not the value used during design when the SCI of the layer is less than 100. The value used is calculated from the relationship (Rollings, R.S., Design of Overlays for Rigid Airport Pavements, Report No. DOT/FAA/PM-87/19, April 1988.):

EExit=E100×[0.02+0.0064(SCIExit)+(0.00584× SCIExit)2]

where,

SCIExist = SCI of the existing PCC layer as it deteriorates during the life of the overlaid structure

EExist = modulus of the existing PCC layer at SCIExist

E100 = modulus of the existing PCC layer when its SCI is 100 (4,000,000 psi in this case)

The modulus of the CTB layer is also set at its default value of 500,000 psi, which is appropriate for design of new structures. But if, from field surveys, the layer is known to be seriously deteriorated, it can be replaced in the representation of the structure by a lower quality layer type or by the variable stabilized layer type with its modulus value set to less than 500,000 psi.

html:

The modulus of the existing PCC surface layer is adjusted during the design, so the value of 4,000,000 psi reported in the design information from the Section Report is an upper limit for the modulus values used in the life computations. Subbase material substitutions are appropriate where there is evidence of serious deterioration from field surveys.
